1.4.src: World Bank Open Data — Food production index (2014-2016 = 100) - Egypt, Arab Rep. (FAO data)
1.4.note: FAO-computed index; WDI series reference period ends 2022, so the latest available observation is three-plus years old. Next level not proposed: Level 4 was not proposed because it requires the index to exceed 115. Egypt's most recent published value, 109.1 for 2022, falls 5.9 index points short of that cut point; no source among those retrieved publishes any Egypt food production index value above 115 for any recent year on the 2014-2016 base. The quoted figure is exactly the WDI/FAO series AG.PRD.FOOD.XD, 'Food production index (2014-2016 = 100)', for Egypt, Arab Rep. — the named construct and the named country. Corroborated by an independent T1 series (World Bank WDI AG.PRD.FOOD.XD): 109.07 for 2022.
1.4.tier_detail: FAO-computed index; WDI series reference period ends 2022, so the latest available observation is three-plus years old

1.2.src: World Bank Open Data — Cereal yield (kg per hectare) (AG.YLD.CREL.KG)
1.2.note: FAO-sourced country data compiled by the World Bank; FAO notes complete cross-country consistency is not possible. Next level not proposed: Level 5 is the top rung, so no higher level exists to be excluded. The one caveat that would matter if a lower rung were in play: the figure is for 2023, not the 2024 reference year available for many other economies, and the World Bank table shows no 2024 value for Egypt, so a more recent observation could not be verified in the supplied pages. The quoted figure is exactly the WDI indicator AG.YLD.CREL.KG, 'Cereal yield (kg per hectare)', for Egypt, Arab Rep., most recent year 2023. The metadata page (databank.worldbank.org) confirms the definition: 'Cereal yield, measured as kilograms per hectare of harvested land, includes wheat, rice, maize, barley, oats, rye, millet, sorghum, buckwheat, and mixed grains.' No construct drift. Corroborated by an independent T1 series (World Bank WDI AG.YLD.CREL.KG): 7402.2 for 2023.
1.2.tier_detail: FAO-sourced country data compiled by the World Bank; FAO notes complete cross-country consistency is not possible

1.1.src: World Bank, World Development Indicators — Agriculture, forestry, and fishing, value added per worker (constant 2015 US$) (NV.AGR.EMPL.KD)
1.1.note: Denominator is an ILO modeled employment estimate (ILOSTAT modeled series); the 2025 figure is the most recent WDI value and is an estimate/projection rather than a final national-accounts outturn. Next level not proposed: Level 5 was not proposed because the top cut point is 10,000 and the published value is 8,942.42 constant 2015 US$ — roughly 1,058 short. No source in the supplied pages publishes an Egypt per-worker figure at or above 10,000 on any basis: the constant-2010 US$ vintage is lower still (7,680 in 2019), and no current-USD per-worker figure for Egypt is published anywhere in these pages, so there is no evidence that an alternative admissible price basis would clear the final threshold. The indicator name reads 'Agriculture value added per worker (USD)'. The only published series for Egypt is WDI NV.AGR.EMPL.KD, whose full title is 'Agriculture, forestry, and fishing, value added per worker (constant 2015 US$)' — i.e. sector scope is ISIC Rev.4 divisions 01-03 (crops and livestock PLUS forestry and fishing), and the price basis is constant 2015 US$, not current USD. Both differences sit on the unratified side of the census question: if the row is later ratified as narrow-agriculture or current-USD, this figure would need replacing. For context on the price-basis gap, WDI reports Egypt's agriculture, forestry and fishing value added in 2025 at 60,456.66 million current US$ (NV.AGR.TOTL.CD), and employment in agriculture at 18% of total employment in 2025 (SL.AGR.EMPL.ZS); no published per-worker figure in current USD was found in the supplied pages. An older constant-2010 US$ vintage of the same series (indexmundi, T5) gives 7,680 for 2019, which is a different price basis again and is not used here. Corroborated by an independent T1 series (World Bank WDI NV.AGR.EMPL.KD): 8942.42 for 2025.
1.1.tier_detail: Denominator is an ILO modelled employment estimate (ILOSTAT modelled series); the 2025 figure is the most recent WDI value and is an estimate/projection rather than a final national-accounts outturn.

1.3.src: World Bank, World Development Indicators — Employment in agriculture (% of total employment) (modeled ILO estimate), Egypt, Arab Rep.
1.3.note: ILO modeled estimate / nowcast for the reference year 2025, not a nationally reported labor force survey observation; WDI metadata warns that 'imputed observations are not based on national data, are subject to high uncertainty, and should not be used for country comparisons or rankings'. Next level not proposed: Level 4 was not proposed because it requires the share to fall below the 15% cut, and the only published figure for Egypt on this construct is 18 (2025, modeled) — three points above that cut. No source in the retrieved pages, official or otherwise, publishes an Egyptian agricultural employment share below 15%; the nearest observed-year value available (18.69% for 2023) is higher still, so the trend gives no basis for treating the 15% threshold as already crossed. The indicator name '1.3 — Employment in agriculture (%)' omits the denominator; the quoted series is explicitly '% of total employment', which is the standard reading and is what is recorded here. Two further gaps between name and evidence: (a) the sector definition is ISIC-A, i.e. 'activities in agriculture, hunting, forestry and fishing' (WDI long definition), so it is broader than agriculture alone; (b) the 2025 figure is an ILO MODELLED estimate/projection, not an observed national statistic, so it should not be carried in the register at a 'Measured' evidence class without that caveat. A nearer-to-observed anchor for the same series is 18.69% for 2023 (reported on tradingeconomics.com, a T5 aggregator of World Bank data, therefore not recorded as the value here); it is materially identical to the 2025 modeled 18. An independent T1 series (World Bank WDI SL.AGR.EMPL.ZS (ILO modeled estimate)) reports 17.52 for 2025, which differs from the value recorded here.
1.3.tier_detail: ILO modelled estimate / nowcast for the reference year 2025, not a nationally reported labour force survey observation; WDI metadata warns that 'imputed observations are not based on national data, are subject to high uncertainty, and should not be used for country comparisons or rankings'

1.6.value: DATA GAP — Read all nine supplied pages in order of likely relevance. (1) IFAD 'Egypt: Smallholder contract farming for high-value and organic agricultural exports' — only front matter and table of contents retrieved; the body tables (domestic market structure, modern retail structure) that might carry a channel share were not in the extracted text, so nothing quotable. (2) and (3) FAO family-farming pages — both returned Cloudflare bot-verification screens, no content. (4) World Bank PID P180480 (2024) — contains the most on-point material, but qualitative: fragmentation 'limiting access to markets for smallholder farmers', plus the 80 percent small-scale farm-unit share; no market-access rate. (5) World Bank value-chain report (2021) — only front matter/TOC in the extract; no smallholder market-access percentage visible. (6) IFC Country Private Sector Diagnostic (2020) — front matter and figure list only; agribusiness section text not in extract. (7) FAO/CIHEAM/CIRAD small-scale family farming Egypt study (2017) — TOC only in extract; sections on cropping patterns and marketing not rendered, so no verifiable figure. (8) Egypt Ministry of International Cooperation news item — project outputs (1,200 farmers contracted, 14,000 target beneficiaries in seven governorates), a project count, not a national rate. (9) Urgenci CSA page — T5, states small-scale farmers are largely absent from Cairo farmers' markets, but no statistic and not an admissible tier for one. Dead end overall: no page in the supplied set publishes a smallholder formal-market-access percentage for Egypt.
1.6.note: Next level not proposed: Not applicable — no level proposed. The specific missing element is any published percentage, range, or ordinal band for the share of Egyptian smallholder farmers accessing formal markets; the strongest source (World Bank 2024) is directional prose only, and the contract-farming participation figure cited in the indicator census is both sub-national and a different construct, and did not appear in the supplied pages for quote verification. Closest available evidence for Egypt: the World Bank Project Information Document for the Climate Resilient Agri-Food Transformation Project (P180480, Apr 2024) states that land fragmentation is 'limiting access to markets for smallholder farmers due to the small volumes produced by the highly fragmented farming units', and that 'Eighty percent of farming units are small-scale, using less than three feddans (approximately 1.5 ha)'. The 80 percent figure is a share of FARM UNITS that are smallholdings — a farm-size-distribution statistic — not a share of smallholders with access to formal markets. The qualitative statement establishes direction (access is constrained) but publishes no rate. Per the unratified-definition note, the indicator NAME asserts national smallholder ACCESS to formal markets; the Egyptian evidence base offers only (a) qualitative constraint statements and (b) sub-national contract-farming PARTICIPATION rates, which are a narrower construct (one contractual channel, seven governorates) and not national access.

1.5.value: No national all-crop post-harvest loss rate is published for Egypt; the available evidence is commodity-specific and mixes loss with waste: a peer-reviewed ICARDA/ARC study estimates that 20.62 percent of Egypt's total w
1.5.src: Sustainability (MDPI), Yigezu et al., 'Food Losses and Wastage along the Wheat Value Chain in Egypt and Their Implications on Food and Energy Security, Natural Resources, and the Environment'; and FAO, 'Food loss and waste in Egypt'
1.5.note: RATIFICATION HOLD — The indicator name asserts an all-crop NATIONAL POST-HARVEST loss rate. The best Egyptian evidence sits on the wrong side of that question in two ways: (a) it is commodity-specific (wheat, grapes, tomatoes, fish), not an all-crop national aggregate; and (b) the headline 20.62 percent wheat figure is a food LOSS AND WASTAGE figure covering the whole life cycle including household/consumer wastage, not post-harvest loss alone. FAO's SDG 12.3.1a Food Loss Index — the nearest official construct, covering harvest to pre-retail — publishes global and regional values in the supplied pages (world 13.3 percent in 2023, sub-Saharan Africa 23.0 percent) but no Egypt country value appears in any page retrieved here. Those global/regional numbers are context only and are not Egypt figures.. The level is withheld and this row leaves every mean. Commodity-specific estimates from value-chain studies; the wheat figure combines losses and consumer-level wastage, and the FAO horticulture figures are explicitly described as preliminary.
1.5.tier_detail: Commodity-specific estimates from value-chain studies; the wheat figure combines losses and consumer-level wastage, and the FAO horticulture figures are explicitly described as preliminary

1.7.value: DATA GAP — 1) Checked all four World Bank Findex 2025 Egypt pages (microdata catalog landing, study description, data dictionary F1, get-microdata) for a rural or agricultural credit statistic — these are metadata and variable listings only; the variable names 'borrowed', 'fin22a', 'urbanicity', 'receive_agriculture' appear but no estimates, and the unit of analysis is the individual adult, not the farmer. 2) Checked the Findex download-data page (worldbank.org) — it describes the availability of rural/urban disaggregation for ~300 indicators but publishes no Egypt value on the page. 3) Checked IFPRI/CGIAR 'An Agricultural Policy Review of Egypt' (T2) — retrieved text is title page, table of contents, acronym list and introduction; PBDAC is named in the acronym list but no credit-access share appears. 4) Checked GIZ Gender Value Chain Assessment (T4) — contents page lists an 'Access to financial credit' section and a sample of 100 farmers in Minya and Beni Suef, but the retrieved text stops before any figure. 5) Checked the Exa publication page on PBDAC/ABE restructuring (T5) — supply-side loan value and credit-covered-area figures only, wrong construct and inadmissible tier for a statistic. Dead ends: no CAPMAS agricultural census page, no Central Bank of Egypt financial-inclusion release, and no FAO/IFAD Egypt rural finance figure was among the supplied pages. Concluding: found=false, ratification hold.
1.7.note: Next level not proposed: The evidence does not establish any farmer-denominated percentage at all, so no cut point — not even the lowest, 10 percent — can be shown to be passed or not passed. Specifically, no source in the retrieved set reports the number or proportion of Egyptian agricultural holders who obtained or could obtain formal agricultural credit; the closest quantities are national adult borrowing variables (no values published on these pages) and supply-side loan/area aggregates. The nearest admissible evidence base for Egypt is the Global Findex 2025 (T1, World Bank), whose Egypt file is described in the retrieved metadata as covering individuals ('UNIT OF ANALYSIS Individual', 'GEOGRAPHIC COVERAGE National Coverage', 1001 cases) with variables 'borrowed', 'fin22a Borrowed from a formal bank or similar financial institution' and a rural/urban breakdown flag 'urbanicity'. Even if a rural sub-population figure were extracted from that source, it would measure (a) adults aged 15+ living in rural areas, a population that includes large numbers of non-farmers, and (b) realised borrowing in the past year, not access to agricultural credit. The indicator's name asserts a share of FARMERS with credit ACCESS, so the Findex series sits on the wrong side of both the population question and the access-vs-use question flagged in the indicator census. Source 9 (an abstract, T5) reports supply-side aggregates for Egypt — total agricultural loans and the area covered by agricultural credit falling from '1.97 billion in 2009/10 acres to 1.07 billion acres in 2019/20' — which is a portfolio/area measure, not a share of farmers, and is in any case not an admissible tier for a statistic.

8.1.src: World Bank, World Development Indicators — Prevalence of undernourishment (% of population), Egypt, Arab Rep. (source: FAO)
8.1.note: World Bank portal displays the FAO series rounded to whole percent (FAO's underlying 2023 figure is reported elsewhere as 9.4%); 2023 values are FAO projections based on nowcasts. Next level not proposed: Level 4 would require Egypt's PoU to be below 7.5%. It is not: the T1 figure is 9 (9.4 unrounded per the FAO-sourced aggregator), and the trend is upward (from 8.8 in 2022), so the 7.5 cut is not passed. The older WHO NLiS profile figure of 4.5% for 2016-2018 is a superseded FAO series vintage — FAO explicitly revises the entire historical series each edition and states only the current series should be used — so it cannot be used to claim a sub-7.5 value. The World Bank series SN.ITK.DEFC.ZS is the FAO prevalence of undernourishment indicator (SDG 2.1.1), national population share whose habitual food consumption is insufficient for dietary energy requirements — exactly the named construct for Egypt. The portal table shows a rounded whole number (9); a T5 aggregator (TheGlobalEconomy, citing FAO) shows the unrounded 9.4 for the same year, which does not change the band. An independent T1 series (World Bank WDI SN.ITK.DEFC.ZS) reports 9.4 for 2023, which differs from the value recorded here.
8.1.tier_detail: World Bank portal displays the FAO series rounded to whole percent (FAO's underlying 2023 figure is reported elsewhere as 9.4%); 2023 values are FAO projections based on nowcasts

1.8.value: DATA GAP — Worked through the nine supplied pages in order. (1) fao.org family-farming raised beds page returned only a Cloudflare bot-verification stub — no text, dead end. (2) FAO STI Portal MRB record: rich adoption narrative and an acreage goal, but ordinal adoption levels only, no farmer share. (3) FAO STI Portal ICARDA integrated wheat bundle: adoption level '3. Project partners' — pilot stage, no share. (4) World Bank MALR programmatic support .docx: retrieved content was 'undefined', no extractable text. (5) FAO SCALA Egypt country page: NAP/NDC narrative, climate impact percentages (15 percent of Delta land affected; wheat and maize productivity declines of 15 and 19 percent by 2050) — impact projections, not adoption. (6) FAO Investment Center Country Investment Highlights No. 22: only front matter and contents were retrieved; Chapter 4 on scaling up climate-smart technologies is listed but its body text, which might carry adoption or scaling-potential figures, is not in the supplied extract, so nothing could be quote-verified. (7) IFPRI/CGSpace CSA policy seminar note: qualitative, describes EWS, contract farming, GIZ field schools, WFP plots — no adoption percentage. (8) Egyptian Ministry of Agriculture economic affairs crop database: page rendered as an empty query form with no returned rows. (9) Ahram Online feature (T5, and in any case statistics not admissible from this tier): quotes emission and yield-impact figures only. Conclusion: no admissible page in this set carries a percentage of farmers using climate-smart practices in Egypt.
1.8.note: Available Egypt CSA evidence is programme-level and qualitative; the one quantified item in the retrieved pages is a government acreage target, not a measured adoption rate, and the STI Portal record is flagged 'Newly extracted from original record - Not checked, not enriched' with AI-assisted extraction. Next level not proposed: Not applicable because no level is proposed. For completeness: nothing in the retrieved pages establishes even the lowest rung, because no source measures the proportion of Egyptian farmers using climate-smart practices — the only quantified item is a 2 million acre government target for one practice on one crop, with no farmer or area denominator. The indicator names the share of FARMERS adopting climate-smart practices. The best available Egypt evidence in these pages sits on the wrong side of the census question in two ways. (1) Unit of measure: the FAO STI Portal record for Mechanized Raised Beds describes integration into 'Egypt's national wheat campaign with a goal of 2 million acres by 2022' — a target LAND AREA under one practice, with no farmer denominator and no verified realised figure. (2) Practice basket and crop scope: it covers a single agronomic practice on a single crop (wheat), whereas the indicator name implies any climate-smart practice across all farmers. The STI Portal also assigns an 'Adoption level 9. Livelihood system (Common)' rating to MRB and 'Adoption level 3. Project partners' to the ICARDA/CGIAR integrated agronomic bundle — ordinal readiness/adoption ladders, not population shares. The FAO Investment Center report (Country Investment Highlights No. 22) prioritises CSA technologies in maize, wheat, date palm and dairy and assesses their 'scaling up potential', which is prospective rather than a measured current adoption rate.

2.4.src: ITU DataHub — Individuals using the Internet (Egypt)
2.4.note: Next level not proposed: The 80% cut point is not passed: the highest published value for Egypt in any supplied source is 74.6% (ITU, 2024) / 75 rounded (World Bank WDI, 2024), so there is no evidence that Internet use reaches or exceeds 80% of individuals, which level 5 would require. ITU defines the indicator as "the proportion of individuals who used the Internet from any location in the last three months", which is exactly the named construct (national, all individuals). The World Bank WDI page (Source 1), which republishes the same ITU series, shows Egypt, Arab Rep. 2024 = 75 (rounded). Corroborated by an independent T1 series (World Bank WDI IT.NET.USER.ZS): 74.65 for 2024.

8.5.note: RATIFICATION HOLD — The published statistic counts female agricultural HOLDERS (the person exercising management control over the holding), not female LAND OWNERS. The Egyptian census reports tenure (owned / rented / other) and sex of holder in separate tables and does not cross-tabulate them, so the share of women among agricultural land owners is not available. 2.1.value: DATA GAP — Order of inspection: (1) ITU DataHub 'About' page — confirmed ITU collects 'mobile population coverage (total, 3G, 4G and above)' from regulators, but the page is methodological and carries no Egypt value and no rural/urban split; dead end for a value. (2) ITU Facts and Figures 2025 landing page — narrative only ('Mobile broadband coverage is nearly universal... urban-rural divides continue to narrow but endure'), no country table, no Egypt figure; dead end. (3) Facts and Figures 2023 and 2022 PDFs as supplied — front matter, forewords and contents only; the 2023 foreword discusses income-group 5G and 3G shares globally, no Egypt row in the retrieved text. (4) Facts and Figures 2021 PDF — foreword notes 'Close to 30 per cent of Africa's rural population still lacks mobile broadband coverage', which is a REGIONAL rural figure for Africa, not Egypt, and rule 5 bars carrying it across a border. (5) MCIT 'Decent Life' page (T3) — describes mobile network coverage expansion in 4,500 villages, no percentage. (6) NTRA news release on Haya Karima (T3) — rural-specific and quantified, but in stations and villages (1096 stations, 899 villages, phase 1), not coverage share. (7) GSMA coverage-maps pages — tool descriptions only, no Egypt figure, and T4 in any case, below the tier floor for this prerequisite. (8) digitaldevelopment.org Egypt page — has 3G 99% / 4G 61% population coverage but national and T5. Not searched/unavailable in the supplied set: ITU DataHub Egypt country page, NTRA quarterly/annual telecom indicator bulletins, CAPMAS ICT statistics, and GSMA Intelligence rural coverage estimates — any of these could plausibly carry the rural split and should be the first stop on re-run.
2.1.note: Next level not proposed: Not applicable at level 0 — no level is asserted. For the record, the specific missing item is a published rural-disaggregated mobile broadband population-coverage percentage for Egypt from ITU DataHub, NTRA, MCIT or CAPMAS; without it, even level 1 cannot be evidenced, since level 1 would itself be a claim that rural coverage is below 20%, which the sources equally fail to show. The closest quantified evidence in the supplied pages is NATIONAL, not rural, and sits at T5: the USAID-affiliated digitaldevelopment.org Egypt page lists 'Population covered by 3G signal: 0.99' and 'Population covered by 4G signal: 0.61' (i.e. 99% and 61% of the total population), plus '3G Coverage: 99.00'. These are national population-coverage shares of the kind the assessment's indicator census flags as the wrong side of the open definitional question: recording an ITU-style national at-least-3G number here would score level 5 mechanically while saying nothing about rural Egypt. Egypt's rural population is roughly 57% of the total, so a national 99% 3G figure is not decomposable into a rural rate without a published disaggregation, and the national 4G figure of 61% implies material sub-national gaps. Separately, the NTRA (T3) release on the 'Haya Karima' rural programme reports rural network build-out in absolute units — 1096 new mobile stations, 594 USF-funded, a 43% increase in stations serving phase-1 villages, 4G voice and mobile internet for 899 phase-1 villages at EGP 4 billion — which is rural-specific but is a deployment count, not a share of rural population covered, and covers only phase 1 of a programme targeting 4,500 villages. Neither the national percentage nor the village/station counts measures 'rural mobile broadband coverage (3G/4G)' as a rate.

2.9.src: World Bank, World Development Indicators — Access to electricity, rural (% of rural population) (EG.ELC.ACCS.RU.ZS)
2.9.note: Modeled/estimated series: World Bank Global Electrification Database compiles nationally representative household survey and census data, with modeling used to fill missing years; rounded to 100.0. The quoted figure is from the World Bank indicator EG.ELC.ACCS.RU.ZS, defined in the metadata glossary as 'the percentage of rural population with access to electricity' — exactly the named rural construct. The corresponding national figure (Access to electricity, % of population) for Egypt is also 100.0 in 2024, but the value recorded here is the rural-specific series, not the national one. Corroborated by an independent T1 series (World Bank WDI EG.ELC.ACCS.RU.ZS): 100 for 2024.
2.9.tier_detail: Modelled/estimated series: World Bank Global Electrification Database compiles nationally representative household survey and census data, with modelling used to fill missing years; rounded to 100.0

2.5.src: ITU DataHub — ICT prices dashboard, Egypt
2.5.note: Value comes from ITU's 2025 price-basket collection under the revised (2024 EGTI) methodology; the 5GB data-only basket replaced the earlier 1.5GB/2GB-era definitions, so the series is not continuous with pre-2025 mobile-broadband affordability figures for Egypt. Next level not proposed: Level 5 would require the value to fall below 1% of monthly GNI per capita. Egypt's 2025 data-only 5GB mobile-broadband basket is 1.58%, and the voice-and-data high-consumption 5GB basket is higher still at 1.92%; only the smaller 1GB voice-and-data basket (0.74%) would clear 1%, and that basket is a voice+data low-consumption bundle rather than a mobile broadband price, so it cannot be used to lift this row to level 5. The indicator name 'Mobile broadband price (% GNI pc)' does not fix the basket allowance, the basket type, or whether the denominator is monthly or annual GNI pc. I have taken ITU's live headline data-only mobile-broadband basket (5GB) as the closest match to 'mobile broadband price', because it is data-only (not voice+data) and is the current published series for Egypt. Its denominator is MONTHLY GNI per capita, per ITU convention — if the row were intended as annual GNI pc the figure would be roughly one twelfth of 1.58. Alternative baskets published for Egypt on the same page for 2025: mobile broadband data-and-voice high-consumption (140 min, 20 SMS, 5 GB) = 1.92%; data-and-voice low-consumption (70 min, 50 SMS, 1 GB) = 0.74%; fixed-broadband 5GB = 2.52%. The 2GB legacy series that the census flags is not present in the retrieved pages, so no 2GB figure could be quoted.
2.5.tier_detail: Value comes from ITU's 2025 price-basket collection under the revised (2024 EGTI) methodology; the 5GB data-only basket replaced the earlier 1.5GB/2GB-era definitions, so the series is not continuous with pre-2025 mobile-broadband affordability figures for Egypt.

2.7.value: DATA GAP — 1) CAPMAS HIECS 2015 metadata page (T1): abstract confirms the survey has a section on 'The possessing of House Appliances, Transportation means, and Communications' with urban/rural breakdown, but the overview page carries no tabulated values and no smartphone-specific item — metadata only, dead end for a figure. 2) ITU/MCIT 2009 conference paper 'ICT Indicators for Households: Egypt's experience' (T1 domain): describes methodology of the biannual 21,000-household ICT survey with urban/rural aggregates, but contains no smartphone ownership statistics at all (predates smartphone measurement). 3) ITU DataHub, Egypt, Location disaggregation: correct rural/urban structure but wrong indicator (households with Internet access at home) and no numeric values in the retrieved text. 4) MCIT Indicators and Publications listing pages (T3): index pages only — the 'ICT Indicators in Brief' and 'Measuring the Digital Society in Egypt' items are download links whose contents were not retrieved, so no value could be quote-verified. 5) GeoPoll blog (T5): gives national mobile-phone ownership (98.8% households / 95% individuals, 2020) — wrong construct on two counts (national, not rural; mobile phones, not smartphones) and an inadmissible tier for a statistic. Conclusion: figure not present in supplied pages; recorded as not found with a ratification hold.
2.7.note: Next level not proposed: Not applicable — no level proposed. The specific missing element is any published rural-disaggregated smartphone ownership percentage for Egypt from CAPMAS, MCIT/ICT Indicators, ITU, GSMA Consumer Survey or a peer-reviewed study. Best available context in the supplied pages: GeoPoll (T5, 2021) reports that for 2020 Egypt's MCIT announced 98.8% of Egyptian households and 95% of individuals owned MOBILE PHONES. That figure is (a) national, not rural; (b) mobile phones of any type, not smartphones; and (c) carried by a news/vendor-tier blog, which may not carry a statistic. The ITU DataHub page retrieved (Households with Internet access at home, Egypt, with Rural/Urban disaggregation) measures household internet access, not smartphone ownership, and no values were present in the page text. On the unratified households-vs-individuals question: even if a rural figure were located from CAPMAS/MCIT household ICT surveys, it would most likely be a rural HOUSEHOLD 'at least one smartphone' share, which sits on the household side of the named individual-ownership construct and reads systematically higher.

2.11.value: Egypt's Ministry of Communications and Information Technology, through the National Telecommunication Institute and Nasser Social Bank, runs the ProGIG initiative providing soft loans of up to EGP 65,000 for purchasing l
2.11.src: Egypt Ministry of Communications and Information Technology — NTI: ProGIG Initiative
2.11.note: Implementer's own programme page; no publication date for the scheme, no independent verification, no reported uptake. Next level not proposed: Operating was not recorded because the retrieved pages contain no evidence that any loan has actually been made: no borrower counts, no disbursed amounts, no start date, no reporting period. Level 4 was not proposed because quality_evidence is empty — the only source is the implementing ministry's own descriptive page, which is design documentation, not an evaluation, audit or performance report; no independent or official assessment of ProGIG appears in the supplied pages. Level 5 was not proposed because scale_evidence is empty — no beneficiary numbers, disbursement totals or geographic spread are published in any retrieved source (the EGP 65,000 figure is a per-borrower ceiling, i.e. a design parameter, not reach). ProGIG is a publicly-sponsored device financing scheme (subsidised/soft loans plus a 50% discount on administrative costs for laptop purchase), so it sits on the 'financing scheme with a public subsidy element' side of the unratified definitional question, not the contested 'commercial telco handset instalment' side. However, its targeting is ICT-training graduates and youth, not farmers or rural households; the indicator name fixes no targeting test, so it is admitted, but nothing in the retrieved pages shows any agriculture- or rural-targeted device financing in Egypt. Adjacent context, not counted: World Bank/MCIT pages describe state-procured educational tablets distributed to secondary students ('the tablets given to them by the Ministry') and a Samsung tablet factory in Beni Suef — a public device provision programme for schools, not a financing/subsidy scheme for rural or agricultural users.
2.11.tier_detail: Implementer's own programme page; no publication date for the scheme, no independent verification, no reported uptake

3.11.value: DATA GAP — 1) CAPMAS Central Data Catalog (T1) — checked whether the national statistical office publishes an agricultural data standard; found only a 629-study NADA/DDI catalog with an Agriculture collection, i.e. a platform metadata standard, no statement of an agricultural interoperability standard. 2) CAPMAS study page for Agricultural Property and Rein 2017 (T1) — study-level documentation only (press release, report), no data standard or schema. 3) FAO AGROVOC 'Semantic data interoperability on food and agriculture' (T2) — the right construct but global; the retrieved text (front matter, contents, acronyms) contains no Egypt-specific adoption or editorial-institution statement, so it is not evidence about this country. 4) Egypt Open Data Policy 2025, National Council for AI (T3) — the strongest quotable instrument, but cross-government and sector-neutral (Annex I metadata standards for open data, data.gov.eg portal, EDGA); does not name agriculture. 5) MCIT ICT Sector Policies 2012-2017 (T3) — lists green ICT, cloud, digital identity, open source, access to information; no agricultural data interoperability policy. 6) Masaar analysis of the Open Data Policy (T5) — inadmissible for a prerequisite cell and in any case discusses general open-data governance, not agricultural standards. Dead ends: nothing in the supplied pages from the Ministry of Agriculture and Land Reclamation, no Egyptian agricultural data dictionary, farmer-registry data model, or e-agriculture interoperability specification.
3.11.note: Next level not proposed: No level proposed at all. Specifically, 'Announced' (level 2) was not reached because no retrieved government document announces an agricultural data standard, interoperability framework or data-exchange specification for the agriculture sector; the only announced instrument is the sector-neutral national Open Data Policy, whose scope section and annexes address government data generally. Context, not recorded as the value: Egypt's national 'Open Data Policy' (National Council for Artificial Intelligence, 2025, ai.gov.eg, T3) is a whole-of-government transitional framework covering open-by-default publication, Open Data Officers, a unified national portal, licensing models and an annex on metadata standards for open data. It is cross-government and sector-neutral — it names no agricultural data model, no crop/livestock/parcel schema, no agri-specific exchange standard, and no MALR-level implementation. This is exactly the open question the indicator census flags: the best available evidence sits on the CROSS-GOVERNMENT side of the agriculture-specific / cross-government line, not the agriculture-specific side. Separately, the CAPMAS microdata catalog (censusinfo.capmas.gov.eg, T1) runs on NADA 4.0 with DDI metadata and holds 629 studies including an Agriculture collection — DDI is a genuine statistical-metadata interoperability standard, but the retrieved page is a catalog listing that states no policy, mandate or standard for agricultural data interoperability, only a platform footer ('Powered by NADA 4.0 and DDI'). FAO's AGROVOC document (T2) is a global FAO product and contains no Egypt-specific statement in the retrieved text.

4.2.note: National regulator reporting its own country's score rather than the ITU report itself; the ITU GCI 2024 report PDF was not among the retrieved pages, so the figure is second-hand from the assessed government. Minor internal inconsistency across sources on Tier 1 membership (NTRA says 47 countries, the ITU-derived press account says 46). Next level not proposed: Level 5 is the top rung, so no higher level was withheld. The residual doubt that would matter to an auditor is directional rather than level-changing: the maximum score is quoted from the assessed government's own regulator, not from the ITU GCI 2024 report itself, which was not retrievable in the supplied pages; and the score measures cybersecurity commitment instruments (laws, strategies, CERT, cooperation), not measured cyber-resilience outcomes or any agriculture-sector-specific cybersecurity provision. The figure is Egypt's ITU Global Cybersecurity Index (GCI) 2024 overall score, which is the construct the indicator names. Two caveats bear on the unratified definition: (a) GCI 2024 is scored out of 100 (five pillars of 20 points each), while this register's cut points (0.2/0.4/0.6/0.8) are written on a 0-1 basis — the two are commensurable only after dividing by 100 (Egypt = 1.00), and the register's Nigeria entry of 0.824 appears to be on the 0-1 scale while Egypt's 100 is on the 0-100 scale; (b) the ITU GCI 2024 pages retrieved here (itu.int publication landing page and the GCI programme page) do not display a per-country overall score, so the only quotable figure for Egypt in the supplied material is the Egyptian regulator's statement of 100 points and Tier 1 ("role modeling") classification. Separately, GCI measures national cybersecurity commitment generally, not agriculture-sector cybersecurity.

4.5.value: DATA GAP — Reviewed all nine supplied pages in order. Sources 1-4 (FAO GSARS news, T1): capacity-building workshops on dissemination, open data standards, microdata anonymisation and CAADP indicator computation with MALR and CAPMAS - activity reports, no governance instrument. Source 5 (FAO microdata catalog, T1): 2009-2010 Agricultural Census metadata, includes a confidentiality declaration requirement referencing CAPMAS, but this is survey access conditions, not a sector data governance framework. Source 6 (FAO NENA regulatory framework paper, T2): regional scope; the supplied extract is front matter and contents only, with no Egypt country section text available to quote. Source 7 (ai.gov.eg Open Data Policy 2025, T3): the strongest governance artifact but cross-sector, with the Data Governance Law still described as forthcoming; no agricultural provisions in the extract. Source 8 (FAOLEX, Sustainable Agricultural Development Strategy toward 2030, T3): agriculture strategy with monitoring and evaluation sections in the table of contents, but the supplied extract is front matter only and contains no data governance text to quote. Source 9 (COMCEC presentation, T5): describes fragmented Egyptian agricultural statistics across MALR Economic Affairs Sector and CAPMAS and calls for unification - a T5 publisher, inadmissible for a prerequisite row and in any case a diagnosis, not a framework. Dead ends: no MALR data policy, no agricultural data-sharing decree, no executive regulations of a Data Governance Law, and no Egypt chapter of the FAO NENA paper were present among the retrieved pages. Any figure or framework claim beyond the above would have to be drawn from text not supplied here, so none is recorded.
4.5.note: Next level not proposed: Not applicable - no level proposed. The specific reason the row is not scored at 3 (Adopted) is that the only adopted instrument in evidence, the 2025 Open Data Policy, governs all public-sector data and contains no agricultural data provisions in the retrieved text; and the reason it is not scored at 2 (Announced) is that no supplied page contains a government announcement of an agriculture-specific data governance framework. Closest available evidence, offered as context only, not as an answer: (1) Egypt's Open Data Policy (National Council for Artificial Intelligence, 2025, T3, ai.gov.eg) sets cross-government open data principles, an Interagency Data Release Board, the Egyptian Data Governance Authority, Open Data Officers, licensing and metadata annexes, and states it applies during a transitional period before enactment of a forthcoming Data Governance Law. It is horizontal public-sector data governance, not an agricultural data governance framework, and the retrieved text names no agriculture sector rules, no farm-data ownership or farmer-consent provisions, and no MALR/CAPMAS agricultural data-sharing arrangement. (2) FAO (2023) 'Regulatory framework for agricultural data in the Near East and North Africa region' is a regional analytical paper whose contents list flags 'Insufficient legal frameworks concerning agricultural data' and 'Deficiencies in current data regulations with respect to agricultural data' for NENA as a whole; the supplied text carries no Egypt-specific determination. (3) FAO GSARS news items describe training workshops on statistical dissemination and data analysis for MALR and CAPMAS staff (2023-2024) and mention discussion of a data dissemination strategy in Egypt, but training activity is not a governance framework and no adopted instrument is named or cited.

Tertiary education' — again all fields, and the extract shows only Afghanistan/Albania rows. 5.3.note: Next level not proposed: Nothing in the supplied evidence shows what fraction of Egyptian tertiary enrollment is in STEM fields, or what a STEM-specific gross enrollment ratio for Egypt would be. Without that, even level 1 cannot be affirmed as a measurement of the named construct rather than as a guess bounded by the all-fields total of 38. Context only, not recorded as the cell value: World Bank WDI 'School enrollment, tertiary (% gross)' (SE.TER.ENRR, https://data.worldbank.org/indicator/SE.TER.ENRR?locations=EG) lists Egypt, Arab Rep. at a most-recent value of 38 for 2025; the female series on the Gender Data Portal gives 38.6% for 2025; IndexMundi (T5 mirror) gives 38.90 for 2018. All of these are the gross enrollment ratio for ALL tertiary education regardless of field — the WDI long definition is 'the ratio of total enrollment, regardless of age, to the population of the age group that officially corresponds to the level of education shown' — with no restriction to science, technology, engineering or mathematics. The indicator name as written asserts the STEM subset; the available evidence sits on the wrong side of that open definitional question. A STEM-specific measure would additionally be a share-of-enrollment or share-of-graduates figure (UIS series such as FOSGP_56_F400), which is a different denominator from a gross enrollment ratio and would not be comparable against the 10/20/30/40 cut points in the same way. 5.4.value: DATA GAP — 1) FAO e-Agriculture Egypt digital extension news (T1) — describes FAO/MoALR digital extension model and farmer awareness sessions; no literacy statistic. 2) FAO geodata farmers' toolkit Egypt page — 404, no content. 3) FAO family farming item — Cloudflare bot-check page, no content. 4) FAO DVI Readiness Assessment — defines a 'digital literacy' criterion for rural communities but is a generic Europe/Central Asia tool with no Egypt value. 5) ITU WSIS+10 Egypt country reporting (T1) — ICT capacity-building narrative across action lines; no farmer digital literacy figure in the retrieved text. 6+7) IFPRI Discussion Paper 02359 full text (CGSpace, T2) — abstract and introduction give intervention effect sizes (uptake +20pp, utilization +26pp, trust +8-13pp), not a literacy stock. 8) IFPRI Policy Note, Sept 2024 (CGSpace, T2) — the only quantified baseline: 52 percent of sampled farmers report general digital literacy as a key challenge; two governorates, ~4,000 GIZ-project farmers; inverse construct, sub-national. 9) OUCI record for Mansour (2023), ICT use among farmers in Qena — 131 farmers, qualitative findings, illiteracy cited as an influence; no percentage. 10) IFPRI Egypt SSP blog (T5) — restates the RCT abstract, effect sizes only. Dead ends: no CAPMAS/MCIT household or agricultural-census digital-skills breakdown for the farming population, and no ITU/Findex rural digital-skills series disaggregated to farmers appeared in the supplied pages. Conclusion: nothing in the retrieved set measures the named construct for Egypt; hold for ratification.
5.4.note: Next level not proposed: Not applicable in the usual sense because no level is proposed; the specific gap is that no source in the retrieved set states, for Egypt, a percentage of farmers assessed or reporting as digitally literate at national scope, in the positive direction the indicator names. Even the lowest rung (below 10 percent) cannot be evidenced, since the sub-national data suggest capability well above that but do not measure it. Indicator names a national percentage of farmers who are digitally literate (higher is better). Closest evidence: IFPRI Policy Note (Sept 2024) / IFPRI Discussion Paper 02359 (Sept 2025) on a randomized digital-literacy intervention in Minya and Beni Suef. Its baseline survey of roughly 4,000 GIZ Agricultural Innovation Project farmers reports that 52 percent named general digital literacy as a key challenge to using mobile applications, 54 percent named unawareness of existing applications, 49 percent lack of smartphone access, and about 65 percent proposed digital literacy training as the remedy. The note also states 2,400 of the 4,000 farmers own smartphones and that non-smartphone owners were excluded from the trial. These are (a) self-reported obstacle rankings, not a tested or assessed literacy rate; (b) framed as illiteracy/barrier prevalence, the inverse of the indicator's H direction; (c) drawn from two Upper Egypt governorates and from members of donor-supported farmer organizations, so not a national farmer population estimate. Contextual only — not recorded as the cell value.

5.8.value: DATA GAP — Worked through all nine supplied pages in order. (1) FAO Egypt 'FAO and MALR launch a Digital Agriculture initiative' (2019): mentions Training of Trainers for MoALR extension personnel and awareness sessions with the Knowledge Economy Foundation — agriculture-situated training but no data-science content, no trainee counts, forward-looking tense. (2) FAO 'Digital education for women's empowerment' (2023): a five-day digital skills course for extension agents in Damas, Dakahlia; anecdotal, two named individuals, no cohort or national pipeline figures, content is basic office/social/app tools. (3) FAO e-Agriculture reprint of the same 2019 launch — duplicate, adds nothing. (4) FAO 'Practical Farmers' Toolkit' link resolves to a 404 error page, no content. (5) FAO Egypt Our Office page: capacity-development language ('increased capacities in technology transfer') but no training-pipeline programme or figures. (6) World Bank 1997 Agricultural Extension and Marketing Assistance Project — a document-details stub from 1997, pre-dating digital agriculture, no usable text. (7) MCIT 'ICT Sector Achievements in 2025': ~500,000 digital capacity-building trainees, 24 innovation hubs, National AI Strategy second edition — all national ICT, agriculture never mentioned. (8) MCIT DEG 2024 graduation release: the fullest description of the national pipeline (DEMI, DECI, DEPI, DEBI) with cohort numbers and named tracks in AI, data analysis, cybersecurity and programming — again no agriculture track. (9) Alliance Bioversity–CIAT 'AgriTech4Egypt Innovation Challenge: Bootcamp report' — the only page that pairs agtech with a training/bootcamp event, but it returned a Cloudflare bot-verification interstitial with no report text, so nothing quotable and nothing on cohort size, curriculum or outcomes. Dead ends: no page in the set links an Egyptian university, technical institute or ministry programme to agricultural data science; no page gives agtech-specific enrollment or graduate counts. Conclusion: named construct not evidenced; hold set.
5.8.note: Ministry self-reported programme figures in a press release; no independent evaluation in the supplied pages. Next level not proposed: No level was proposed at all. Specifically, level 3+ was not proposed because no supplied page shows an adopted or operating training programme that names agriculture, agrifood or agtech as a track, specialisation, cohort or partner; and quality_evidence was withheld because the only performance language available is the Ministry's own statement that 'standards and criteria are being developed to ensure training quality' — a statement of intent about design, not an evaluation or audit result. Scale_evidence was withheld because the published reach figures (13,800 DEPI graduates; ~500,000 digital capacity-building trainees) are reach for a construct other than the one named. The named construct is an agtech/data-science training pipeline. What is published for Egypt in these pages is (a) a generic national data/ICT talent pipeline with no agricultural component and (b) agricultural digital-literacy training with no data-science component. For context only, and quoted exactly from the MCIT pages: 'Furthermore, 13,800 out of 25,000 individuals were trained within the Digital Egypt Pioneers Initiative (DEPI). It aims to enhance the digital skills of university students and graduates across different specializations by delivering specialized educational tracks in Artificial Intelligence (AI), data analysis, cybersecurity, and programming.' and 'Around 500,000 trainees received digital capacity-building training during FY 2024-25, with a target of reaching 800,000 trainees in the current fiscal year.' Neither statement mentions agriculture, agrifood, agronomy or an agtech track. On the other side of the slash, FAO Egypt reports 'Training of Trainers (ToT) programs on the thematic areas and use of the mobile application will be delivered to MoALR extension personnel' and a five-day digital skills course for extension agents covering 'Word, YouTube, e-mail, Facebook, WhatsApp, Zoom and the FAO app El Mufeed' — agriculture-situated, but digital literacy rather than data science, and with no enrollment, graduate or pipeline figures. If the slash is later ratified as disjunctive (either half suffices), the MCIT DEPI evidence would support an Operating rung with scale; if conjunctive (an agtech-specific data-science pipeline), the supplied evidence supports Absent-to-Announced. That fork is exactly the unresolved question flagged in the indicator census, so no level is proposed.

(6) FAO AGRIS record for IFPRI MENA WP 43 on Mahsoly (T1 host, T2 content) — smallholder farmers, constraints to adoption, no percentage. (7) GIZ Gender Value Chain Assessment Egypt (T4) — retrieved text is only the table of contents; a section 'Access to information technology and mobile usage' exists but its content was not in the retrieved pages. (8) ScienceDirect digital-literacy article — blocked by captcha, no text. (9) Ahram Online (T5) — carries the 53% digital-payments figure; recorded as context in construct_note, not usable as the value. Dead ends: no CAPMAS or MCIT ICT-use-by-enterprises release, and no MSMEDA or Visa primary document, was among the retrieved pages; the 53% therefore could not be traced to its publisher for tier upgrade.
6.13.note: Next level not proposed: Level 1 was not proposed either, because proposing it would assert that agribusiness/SME digital tool adoption in Egypt is below 10%, and nothing in the retrieved evidence establishes that: ICARDA reports that two of eight digital-agriculture tool categories (sensors and mobile apps) are already 'fairly widely used', and the (inadmissible) SME payments figure is 53%. The specific missing item that any level would require is a published, tier-admissible adoption rate whose denominator is Egyptian SMEs or agribusiness firms and whose numerator is use of digital tools. Best available quantified evidence: Ahram Online (T5, 16 Sep 2025) reports a Visa/MSMEDA study finding 'Around 53 percent of SMEs have integrated digital payments' in Egypt, with 77% of SME owners expecting electronic transactions to be central to growth. That figure (a) is economy-wide SMEs, not agribusiness firms, (b) covers digital payments only, not the broader 'digital tools' the indicator names, and (c) reaches us only through a news outlet, i.e. an inadmissible tier for a statistic. A second partial measure, World Bank Enterprise Survey 2008 for Egypt (T1), shows 421 of 1,156 firms (36.4%) regularly using a website in interactions with clients, but the ES universe explicitly excludes agriculture ('non-agricultural formal private economy', and the 2025 round covers ISIC Rev.4 10-33 manufacturing plus listed services), the page itself warns the counts 'cannot be interpreted as summary statistics of the population of interest', and the figure is 17 years old. Neither sits on the agribusiness side of the undefined slash.

6.14.src: Central Bank of Egypt — "Financial Inclusion Rates Continue to Surge .. 79% of Citizens Own Active Accounts that Enable Them to Perform Financial Transactions"
6.14.note: RATIFICATION HOLD — The quoted CBE text names smallholder farmers specifically (a project titled "Transforming the Livelihoods of Smallholder Farmers" cited as a leading vehicle of financial inclusion implementation), but it does not state what financial rails the project delivers, whether they are digital/agri-specific, or how many smallholders use them. 3.10.value: Farmer-facing agricultural e-commerce platforms are operating in Egypt, including Nile, a B2B online marketplace that connects fresh produce growers directly with commercial buyers, and Bashaier, a mobile marketplace lin
3.10.src: FAO Science, Technology and Innovation (STI) Portal / ATIO Knowledge Base — "Nile online marketplace" innovation record
3.10.note: FAO STI Portal record is a federated entry harvested from Digital Agri Hub and enriched by automated AI extraction; the page itself states "Newly extracted from original record - Not checked, not enriched", so the platform description is not independently verified by FAO staff. Next level not proposed: Level 4 was not proposed because no independent or official evaluation, audit, service-standard report or performance assessment of any Egyptian agricultural e-commerce platform appears in the retrieved pages. The FAO STI Portal readiness/adoption narratives are AI-generated restatements of the platforms' own descriptions (the page itself flags "Harvested + Automated AI", "Not checked, not enriched"), which is design/self-description, not quality evidence. The only independent analytical text retrieved, the IFPRI/CGIAR policy note, speaks to the digital-agriculture app ecosystem as a whole rather than evaluating e-commerce platform performance, and its finding is that "many Egyptian digital tools remain pilot-stage or region-specific, with very few achieving national scale" — the opposite of a positive performance record. Level 5 was not proposed because no published reach figures (registered growers, transaction volumes, geographic coverage) exist for the farmer-facing platforms in these pages; the only reach numbers available belong to Cartona, a T5 vendor page for a retailer-facing FMCG marketplace, which is inadmissible both on tier and on construct. The indicator census asks whether the row counts only farmer-facing platforms or any agri-food value-chain commerce platform. The evidence quoted (Nile) sits on the farmer-facing side: growers list produce and sell directly to commercial buyers. The second FAO record (Bashaier, https://sti-portal.fao.org/innovations/kef-bashaier-egypt) is likewise farmer-facing. The only Egyptian platform in the retrieved pages with published reach figures is Cartona (cartona.com, T5 vendor page: "150,000+ RETAIL USERS", "4,500+ SUPPLIERS", "18 CITIES"), but Cartona is an FMCG retailer-to-wholesaler B2B marketplace serving mom-and-pop stores, i.e. downstream agri-food trade rather than a farmer-facing agricultural platform, and it is a vendor self-report at T5, which may carry existence facts but not statistics. No figures for Nile or Bashaier were found in the retrieved pages.
3.10.tier_detail: FAO STI Portal record is a federated entry harvested from Digital Agri Hub and enriched by automated AI extraction; the page itself states "Newly extracted from original record - Not checked, not enriched", so the platform description is not independently verified by FAO staff.

3.9.value: Digital agricultural advisory platforms are operating in Egypt (FAO's El Mufeed app launched 2019, the AI-based Hudhud farmer assistant piloted in 2021, and the Bashaier app), but a 2025 IFPRI policy note finds that many
3.9.src: IFPRI/CGIAR Policy Note, 'Digital Agricultural Technology in Egypt: Insights from App Developers' (Abdallah, Abdelhadi and Karachiwalla, December 2025)
3.9.note: Qualitative, interview-based policy note; contains no user counts, registration figures or coverage statistics for any named Egyptian advisory platform. Next level not proposed: Level 4 was not proposed because no independent or official evaluation, audit or performance report on how well any Egyptian advisory platform works appears in the retrieved evidence — the FAO Country Cases and STI Portal entries are implementer/self-reported descriptions (the STI Portal adoption narratives are explicitly AI-generated and in one case state that the underlying description is empty), and the only independent assessment (IFPRI) is negative about scaling, not a positive performance finding. Level 5 was not proposed because no reach figures at all are published for Egypt in these sources: no user counts, no farmer numbers, no governorate coverage. The GSMA AgriTech Accelerator figure of 'over 335,000 new farmers' belongs to a ten-agritech cohort across Africa and Asia that does not include Egypt and cannot be carried across the border. The indicator names 'digital advisory platforms AT SCALE'. The retrieved evidence establishes existence and operation of advisory platforms (El Mufeed, Hudhud, Bashaier, GeoAgro-Misr) but the only source that speaks directly to the scale question does so negatively: it states most Egyptian tools remain pilot-stage or region-specific with very few reaching national scale. No source in this set publishes a registered-user, active-user or farmers-reached figure for any Egyptian advisory platform, so the unratified '>10k user' bar cannot be tested either way. The one large number in the retrieved pages — '2 million cards were distributed to farmers' for the smart farmer card (Daily News Egypt, T5) — is a subsidy/identity card, not an advisory platform, and is a news source and therefore inadmissible for a statistic.
3.9.tier_detail: Qualitative, interview-based policy note; contains no user counts, registration figures or coverage statistics for any named Egyptian advisory platform

7.2.src: Daily News Egypt — Government launches AI-enabled system to enhance agriculture process
7.2.note: RATIFICATION HOLD — the only source is T5 news, vendor or market material, which carries existence facts but never a statistic. The level is withheld and this row leaves every mean. Existence fact only, sourced from a news outlet (T5); no official government artifact, evaluation or usage statistic was retrieved.
