7.12.value: Egypt has adopted a cross-sector responsible-AI safeguards regime — the Egyptian Charter for Responsible AI (2023, National Council for AI) and the National AI Governance Framework (ECRAI/NCAI, March 2026) — which assert
7.12.src: National Council for Artificial Intelligence (Egypt), Egyptian Charter for Responsible AI, 2023 v1.0 (ai.gov.eg)
7.12.note: Non-binding charter; the Charter itself states most such international guidelines are non-binding and that it is a "soft launch". Next level not proposed: Operating was not proposed: the retrieved pages contain only statements of what the instruments require (e.g. that government AI projects 'should be supervised by' MCIT and that MCIT 'presents periodically a report'), which is design language in a non-binding charter, with no retrieved record of a completed impact assessment, an enforcement action, a redress case, or a compliance report actually produced. Even if Operating were granted, the mechanical level would remain 3. Level 4 was not proposed because no independent or official evaluation, audit or performance report on how well these safeguards function was found in the supplied pages — the UNESCO AI Readiness Assessment for Egypt (2025) exists but its full text is not available on the UNESDOC notice page, so nothing could be quote-verified. Level 5 was not proposed because no reach figures (entities covered, assessments conducted, systems registered) are published in these pages. The evidence sits on the cross-sector side of the unresolved definitional question. The Charter and the 2026 National AI Governance Framework are economy-wide instruments issued by the National Council for AI / ECRAI; nothing in the retrieved pages establishes agriculture- or farmer-specific consent or data-rights safeguards (e.g. consent for farm data collection, farmer data ownership). The Charter's rights language covers end-users of AI systems generally; 'consent' as such is not articulated in the quoted Charter text and is carried instead by the Personal Data Protection Law, which the Framework lists as a foundation but which was not retrieved here. If the indicator is later ratified as requiring agriculture-specific safeguards, this row should fall to Absent.
7.12.tier_detail: Non-binding charter; the Charter itself states most such international guidelines are non-binding and that it is a "soft launch"

8.4.value: DATA GAP — 1) World Bank data portal page for FX.OWN.TOTL.YG.ZS (Egypt) — this is combined financial-institution-or-mobile-money account ownership for young adults, a different indicator, and the page carried no numeric Egypt value in the retrieved text. 2) World Bank Gender Data Portal 'Mobile money account (% age 15+)' — correct construct family and contains an Egypt 2024 row, but the rendered table is the women-only series (Sex filter = Female); no Total column values were present in the retrieved text. 3) Findex 2021 glossary and 2021 microdata codebook — confirm the definition of 'mobile money account' (used mobile money services to pay bills or send/receive money in the past year) but contain no Egypt values. 4) Findex 2021 and Findex 2025 Egypt microdata catalog entries — study metadata only, no indicator values. 5) NTRA press releases Q1 and Q2 2025 (T3 regulator) — mobile wallet counts (43.7m, 46.3m), transaction volumes and values; supply-side, not a share of adults. 6) Statista page (T5) — Egypt 2024 mobile money account ownership by gender, value paywalled and in any case not admissible for a statistic. 7) AUC thesis link — CAPTCHA wall, no text. Dead end: no retrieved page carries the total-population Findex figure for Egypt, so the cell is held rather than filled from the female subgroup.
8.4.note: Only sex-disaggregated (female) Findex value available in retrieved pages; regulator figures are wallet counts, not survey-based account ownership shares. Next level not proposed: No supplied page states the total (all adults, 15+) mobile money account percentage for Egypt; the Findex country-level series value for Egypt 2024 on this indicator was not retrieved, and the Gender Data Portal page displays only the female-filtered series. Named construct = share of adults (15+) with a mobile money account. Available evidence: (a) World Bank Gender Data Portal table, source Global Findex, lists Egypt, Arab Rep. for 2024 under the column 'Mobile money account, women (% age 15+)' with the Sex filter set to Female — a women-only subgroup value of 7.8%, not the total-population figure the indicator names; (b) NTRA (Egyptian regulator) reports 46.3 million active mobile wallets nationwide in Q2 2025 and 43.7 million in Q1 2025 — a supply-side count of wallets (multiple wallets/inactive wallets possible, denominator not adult population), which is a different construct from demand-side survey account ownership; (c) Statista (T5) states the share was 'minimal' and that ownership was higher among men than women, but paywalls the number. Because male ownership is higher than the 7.8% female figure, the true total plausibly sits near the first cut point of 10, so no level can be assigned without the published total.

8.2.src: World Bank Open Data — Account ownership at a financial institution or with a mobile-money-service provider, female (% of population ages 15+), Egypt, Arab Rep. (Global Findex Database)
8.2.note: Nationally representative demand-side sample survey (Global Findex 2025 / Gallup World Poll), n=1,001 adults for Egypt; subject to sampling error and to a break in comparability with earlier rounds (2021 female value 24.2%). Next level not proposed: Level 4 would require female account ownership above 60%. The published 2024 value is 40.21%, roughly 20 percentage points short, and no supplied source shows any female account-ownership figure for Egypt above 60% — the highest ever recorded in the series is the 2024 value itself. Even the Central Bank of Egypt's broader administrative-data measure of overall financial inclusion (64.8% of all eligible adults, 2022) is a total, not a female rate, and cannot be used to lift this row. The indicator name is "Account ownership, female (%)" and the quoted WDI series FX.OWN.TOTL.FE.ZS is female-specific (women ages 15+), so the gender construct is matched exactly. On the unratified definitional question: this series is "account at a financial institution OR with a mobile-money-service provider", i.e. mobile-money accounts are counted inside the total, which is the same construct scored separately at 8.4 — so the value sits on the broad side of the open question and mobile money is double-weighted in the FIN column. A narrower financial-institution-only female series (FX.OWN.TOTL.FE.ZS excludes nothing; the FIN.OWN variant) was not among the supplied pages, so no narrower female figure could be quote-verified. Contextual figures NOT used: national all-adult account ownership; and the Central Bank of Egypt (T3) reports 18.3 million women owning a transactional account at end-2022 without publishing a female percentage of adult women, so it cannot substitute for the named percentage. Corroborated by an independent T1 series (World Bank WDI FX.OWN.TOTL.FE.ZS (Global Findex wave)): 40.21 for 2024.
8.2.tier_detail: Nationally representative demand-side sample survey (Global Findex 2025 / Gallup World Poll), n=1,001 adults for Egypt; subject to sampling error and to a break in comparability with earlier rounds (2021 female value 24.2%).

8.6.value: Brookings (World Bank Global Findex/Gallup World Poll data) reports that Egypt is among the economies where the gender gap in mobile phone ownership is about 15 percentage points or larger; no country-specific point esti
8.6.src: Brookings — Mobile phones are key to economic development. Are women missing out? (Leora Klapper)
8.6.note: Egypt is named only inside a group of countries; the page gives a lower bound ('about 15 percentage points or larger'), not an Egypt-specific point estimate. Underlying data are Gallup World Poll / Global Findex survey estimates for adults 15+, not an ITU/NSO official series. Next level not proposed: Level 3 would require evidence that Egypt's absolute gap is at or below 10 percentage points; nothing in the retrieved sources shows that — the only Egypt figure is a floor of roughly 15 pp, half again above the level-3 cut, and no more recent Egypt-specific sex-disaggregated ownership rates (ITU/CAPMAS) were obtained that could demonstrate narrowing since 2018. Conversely the level is not withheld entirely because the phrase 'or larger' is open-ended and could in principle place Egypt above 20 pp (level 1); the '15 percentage points' anchor is treated as the central estimate, and this ambiguity is flagged rather than resolved. The construct named by the indicator is an absolute gender gap in phone ownership expressed in percentage points (male ownership rate minus female ownership rate), and the Brookings figure is exactly that unit and basis (it contrasts, in the same sentence, the relative framing used for Pakistan). It therefore sits on the correct side of the unratified definitional question. Note the alternative widely quoted figure — GSMA's mobile ownership gender gap — is a RELATIVE gap on a male-ownership base (GSMA 2024 reports 8% across LMICs and 82% of women in MENA owning a mobile phone); those are different numbers on a different basis and no Egypt-specific GSMA value appears in the supplied pages. ITU pages supplied carry only global/regional figures (globally 78% of females vs 87% of males aged 10+, i.e. a 9 pp global gap in 2025), not Egypt.
8.6.tier_detail: Egypt is named only inside a group of countries; the page gives a lower bound ('about 15 percentage points or larger'), not an Egypt-specific point estimate. Underlying data are Gallup World Poll / Global Findex survey estimates for adults 15+, not an ITU/NSO official series.

8.9.value: No publisher reports a national percentage of Egyptian smallholders reached by digital services; the available Egypt-specific evidence (IFPRI, 2025) is qualitative, stating that most Egyptian digital agricultural tools r
8.9.src: IFPRI (CGIAR) Policy Note — Digital Agricultural Technology in Egypt: Insights from App Developers
8.9.note: qualitative finding only; no published national percentage, no denominator of Egyptian smallholders, and no definition of 'reached' (registered vs active vs benefiting). Next level not proposed: Level 2 would require documented evidence that at least 10% of Egypt's smallholders are reached by digital services — i.e. an active- or registered-user count for Egyptian digital agricultural services set against a national smallholder denominator, or an official/nationally representative survey estimate of smallholder use. No such count, denominator, or survey estimate appears in any supplied source; the only quantified reach numbers available are LMIC-wide (World Bank Playbook), a non-Egypt programme total (GSMA, 335,000 farmers across Africa and Asia), or experimental treatment effects from a two-governorate RCT, none of which can be converted into a national Egyptian share. The evidence is about the named population (Egyptian smallholder farmers) and the named service class (digital agricultural tools/services), but it is qualitative rather than a published share. The indicator's name asserts a national share; nothing in the supplied pages provides one. Context figures that do NOT answer this cell: (a) the Egypt RCT (Abdelaziz & Abay, Food Policy) reports that 'the standard digital training alone increased uptake by 20 percentage points and utilization by 18 percentage points' — these are experimental treatment effects in a study sample, not a national coverage share, and the paper states 'In Egypt, the focus of this study, uptake of these technologies remains low'; (b) the World Bank DAR Playbook reports '<10% of potential end-users in LMICs use digital ag tools' and '>150 million smallholder farmers in developing countries do not have access to digital services' — both are LMIC-wide, not Egypt; (c) GSMA's AgriTech Accelerator reports 'reaching over 335,000 new farmers' across ten agritechs in Africa and Asia, none of them in Egypt. On the unratified definition question, the best available evidence sits on the wrong side of the indicator's name: it is programme/qualitative evidence, not a national share of smallholders reached.
8.9.tier_detail: qualitative finding only; no published national percentage, no denominator of Egyptian smallholders, and no definition of 'reached' (registered vs active vs benefiting)

8.12.value: DATA GAP — Read all ten supplied pages in order. Sources 1, 2, 3, 5 and 10 (IFAD IOE country strategy and programme evaluations 2017 and 2025, the 2025 slide deck, and the UNEG record of the West Noubaria project performance evaluation) are Egypt-specific and do report income and productivity impacts, but exclusively for irrigation, extension, rural finance and social-infrastructure interventions; the 2025 CSPE mentions digital only as a gap in smallholder services. Source 4 is a 2016 approach paper with no results. Source 6 (IFPRI Egypt SSP) lists publications and blogs but no digital-agriculture yield/income impact figure for Egypt. Source 7 (Forsa midline) evaluates an economic inclusion cash/asset programme, not digital agriculture, and its reported results concern livestock ownership. Source 8 (ClinicalTrials.gov registration of the FAS/IMCHN impact evaluation in Upper Egypt) names household income as an outcome but is Withdrawn with enrollment 0 and no results posted, and the intervention is agribusiness support, not digital. Source 9 is the only page carrying yield and income effect sizes for digital information interventions, and it explicitly lists its study geography as fifteen Sub-Saharan Africa, four India, one Cambodia - no Egypt. Dead ends: no page from MALR, the Agricultural Research Center, ITIDA, or a Digital Egypt / smart-farming programme evaluation was supplied, and no evaluation of an Egyptian agri-advisory platform with a yield or income endpoint appears anywhere in the set. Concluded found=false with a ratification hold.
8.12.note: Next level not proposed: Level withheld rather than set at any rung: the pages retrieved neither confirm the existence of an Egyptian digital-agriculture impact study with a yield or income endpoint (which would support Adopted/Operating) nor constitute a search wide enough to conclude absence (which would support Absent at level 1). Filling quality_evidence with the IFAD CSPE, or scale_evidence with its US$646.3 million portfolio and 41 km of canals, would add two levels on evidence about non-digital rural development, so both fields are left empty. The indicator names documented yield or income impact evidence, understood within a digital-agriculture maturity assessment as impact of digital agricultural services. The best Egypt-specific evidence available in the retrieved pages is the IFAD Independent Office of Evaluation Country Strategy and Programme Evaluation (EC 2025/129/W.P.3 and its slide deck), which reports that IFAD-financed projects contributed to increased household income and improved food security over 2017-2023 across a US$646.3 million portfolio. That is an income outcome, but the interventions evaluated are canal rehabilitation, drip irrigation conversion, farmer field schools, rural finance and social infrastructure - not digital agriculture. Conversely, the RTI meta-analysis in Global Food Security quantifies yield (+6%) and income (+6%) effects of digital information interventions, but its 20 studies are fifteen from Sub-Saharan Africa, four from India and one from Cambodia, so it carries no Egyptian observation and cannot be transferred across the border. The census's own open question - that Egypt's level 3 rests on an evaluation measuring diffusion and adoption of digital tools rather than yield or income - is confirmed by what these pages contain: no Egyptian digital-agriculture evaluation with a yield or income endpoint surfaced.

8.11.value: DATA GAP — 1) CAPMAS microdata/metadata catalog (T1) — checked the GENERAL_PUBLICATIONS collection listing (11 studies, Egypt in Figures and Statistical Yearbooks 2010-2017); no study or variable relating to language of service delivery; dead end. 2) UN DESA EGOVKB Egypt country page (T1) — reviewed EGDI, EPART, Online Service Index, TII and HCI series; the OSI is the nearest sub-index touching online service features, but the country page publishes only the composite value (0.70016 for 2024) with no local-language sub-question disclosed; dead end for the named construct. 3) UN DESA Data Center 2024 EGDI table (T1) — confirms Egypt's rank 95 / 0.6699 but is a cross-country ranking table with no language field; dead end. 4) MCIT press release 'ICT Sector Achievements in 2025' in both English and Arabic (T3) — the most substantive Egyptian government artifact retrieved; enumerates Digital Egypt platform services, users, transactions, apps, exclusive digital services and postal outlets, but contains no statement about local-language availability of services and no share; the existence of the Arabic edition evidences Arabic-language government communication, not a measured localisation rate. 5) GHDx record for Egypt Statistical Yearbook 2023 (T5) — bibliographic stub only, no tables surfaced, and T5 could not carry a statistic in any case. Not available in the supplied pages and would be needed to close this cell: a MALR/Digital Egypt agricultural advisory service inventory disaggregated by interface language, or a UN E-Government Survey questionnaire-level (MSQ) extract showing Egypt's response on local-language service provision.
8.11.note: Next level not proposed: Every level, including level 1, requires a figure (or bounded qualitative finding) about the share of services delivered in local languages. The retrieved pages establish only that Egypt operates a national digital service platform with a growing service count and publishes official communications in Arabic; they do not establish what fraction of agricultural or government digital services is available in local languages, nor any range from which such a fraction could be bounded. The named construct is a percentage share of services available in local languages. The best available evidence in the supplied pages is (a) MCIT's press release on 2025 ICT achievements, which is itself published in both Arabic and English and reports that the Digital Egypt platform offered 210 government digital services to 10.7 million users, and (b) UN DESA's Online Service Index for Egypt (0.70016 in 2024). Both are counts/indices of service availability, not language-of-delivery shares, and neither is agriculture-specific. This sits squarely on the wrong side of the unratified definitional question: no Egyptian publisher supplies a denominator (total services) paired with a numerator (services offered in local languages), so the %-share framing of 8.11 cannot be satisfied from published Egyptian sources. Note also that Egypt's linguistic situation differs from the multilingual case the indicator implicitly targets — Modern Standard Arabic is the official and near-universal national language — which is a further reason the %-share formulation may not be meaningful here, but that is a definitional argument, not published evidence, and cannot be scored.

8.17.value: DATA GAP — Worked through the nine supplied pages in order. (1) FAO WaPOR catalog entry for 'Global outlook on climate services in agriculture' — confirms an Egypt case study exists in the 2024 report but the landing page carries no figure; the report PDF itself was not among the supplied pages. (2) and (3) FAO 'Practical Farmers' Toolkit' and FAO policy-support resource page for the Global Outlook — both returned 404 error pages, dead ends. (4) FAO/WMO agrometeorological services feature — global narrative on the 'last mile' gap, names Cambodia, the Philippines and the Greater Horn of Africa, no Egypt figure. (5) FAO GSARS workshop news for Egypt — agricultural statistics capacity building, unrelated to advisory reach. (6) World Bank PID P180480 — read for a results-framework reach target; the text supplied stops mid-sectoral-context and contains only the PDO wording on early warning services plus poverty and farm-structure statistics, no advisory coverage figure. (7) FAO 'Advancing rural advisory services... in Egypt' policy brief — the most on-topic national document; searched for any extension coverage rate and found only the qualitative 'weakened coverage' formulation, plus demographic and poverty percentages. (8) Sustainability 11(3) 685 — supplies 51.9% but for climate-change knowledge in two governorates, not advisory receipt; logged as context in construct_note rather than as the value. (9) WMO WWIS Egypt — supply-side only, ten cities with EMA forecasts. Conclusion: figure not present in supplied pages; recorded as abstain rather than fabricating a reach percentage.
8.17.note: Next level not proposed: Not applicable — level withheld rather than proposed. The specific missing item is any published national estimate of the percentage of Egyptian farmers or agricultural households receiving climate/weather advisories; without it even level 1 cannot be evidenced, since level 1 asserts a measured value below 20 rather than an absence of measurement. The indicator names climate advisory REACH — the share of farmers receiving climate/weather advisories. The only percentages in the retrieved pages are: (a) a peer-reviewed study (Sustainability 11(3), 685) reporting that 51.9% of 792 surveyed farmers in two Nile Delta governorates had no knowledge of the climate change phenomenon — that is climate-change awareness among a two-governorate sample, not national receipt of advisories, and it is not the inverse of advisory reach either; and (b) FAO's Egypt rural advisory services policy brief, which describes 'weakened coverage of extension and rural advisory services' qualitatively with no coverage percentage and no climate-specific breakdown. On the census's open question, everything available for Egypt sits on the SUPPLY side (WMO WWIS lists official forecasts for ten Egyptian cities via the Egyptian Meteorological Authority; the World Bank Climate Resilient Agri-Food Transformation Project P180480 aims 'to strengthen the nation-wide agriculture information system and early warning services'), i.e. issuance and platform existence, not farmer receipt. FAO's Global Outlook on Climate Services in Agriculture (2024) surveys 36 countries and includes an Egypt case study, but the retrieved page is a catalog landing page and carries no Egypt reach figure in the text supplied.

A1-CAND-IMP.value: DATA GAP — 1) FAO GIEWS Country Brief on Egypt (T1): checked for a dependency ratio; it reports cereal import requirements in tonnes (29 million tonnes for 2026/27; wheat 13.5 Mt; maize 15.5 Mt) — volume, not ratio, so rejected under the construct rule. 2) UNdata mirror of FAOSTAT item 21035, the exact named indicator (T1): Egypt appears in the country filter list and 19 three-year windows (2000-2002 through 2018-2020) are available, but the rendered rows in the retrieved text cover only Afghanistan, Africa and Albania; no Egypt row is present, so no verbatim Egypt figure exists to quote. 3) FAOSTAT landing page (T1) and the FAO catalog metadata record for the Suite of Food Security Indicators (T1): both are descriptive/metadata only, carrying no country values. 4) OECD 'Policies for the Future of Farming and Food in Egypt' (T2): qualitative statements on import concentration and undernourishment (9.4% in 2022-24) but no cereal import dependency ratio. 5) CGSpace FAO presentation 'Food security in Egypt' (T2): names the indicator and shows a chart for Egypt, but the extracted text carries only axis labels (0-70), no data point. 6) Heliyon article on Egyptian wheat import dependency (via PMC): abstract-level content on wheat, not the cereal import dependency ratio. 7) Food Systems Dashboard indicator table: blocked by a Vercel security checkpoint, no data returned. Conclusion: the value almost certainly exists in FAOSTAT's Suite of Food Security Indicators for Egypt, but it is not present in any supplied page and must not be reconstructed from memory.
A1-CAND-IMP.note: Correct indicator series identified at T1 (FAOSTAT via UNdata), but the country-specific row for Egypt was not present in the retrieved page text; series shown is a 3-year average, latest window 2018-2020. Next level not proposed: Not applicable — proposed_level is 0 by design for carried candidate indicators, and additionally no verifiable Egypt value was recoverable from the supplied pages. The four World Bank Findex pages (Sources 1-6) are catalogue metadata and variable dictionaries only: they list variables such as 'borrowed', 'fin22a Borrowed from a formal bank or similar financial institution' and 'urbanicity Respondent lives in rural area', but publish no estimates at all, and in any case the Findex unit of analysis is stated as 'Individual' with 'National Coverage' — rural adults 15+, not farmers, and borrowing behaviour rather than credit access. The IFPRI policy review (Source 7) and the GIZ gender value-chain assessment (Source 8) mention agricultural credit institutions (PBDAC/Agricultural Bank of Egypt) and a section headed 'Access to financial credit', but the retrieved text contains only front matter and contents pages with no percentage. Source 9 is an Exa abstract page (T5) reporting loan values and credit-covered area, not a share of farmers. Because no quote-verifiable value for the named construct exists in the supplied pages, a ratification hold is set rather than a substituted proxy.
answer.construct_note: The nearest admissible evidence base for Egypt is the Global Findex 2025 (T1, World Bank), whose Egypt file is described in the retrieved metadata as covering individuals ('UNIT OF ANALYSIS Individual', 'GEOGRAPHIC COVERAGE National Coverage', 1001 cases) with variables 'borrowed', 'fin22a Borrowed from a formal bank or similar financial institution' and a rural/urban breakdown flag 'urbanicity'. Even if a rural sub-population figure were extracted from that source, it would measure (a) adults aged 15+ living in rural areas, a population that includes large numbers of non-farmers, and (b) realised borrowing in the past year, not access to agricultural credit. The indicator's name asserts a share of FARMERS with credit ACCESS, so the Findex series sits on the wrong side of both the population question and the access-vs-use question flagged in the indicator census. answer.quality_evidence: No demand-side survey of Egyptian farmers reporting credit access was located in the supplied pages. The only T1 survey instrument present (Findex) is nationally representative of adults, sample 1001, with no farmer identifier beyond 'receive_agriculture Received a payment for the sale of agricultural goods'.
answer.scale_evidence: None available: no denominator of farmers or agricultural holdings is paired with a credit-access numerator in any supplied page.
answer.rung_argument: No level is proposed. answer.abstain_reason: No admissible T1-T3 source among the retrieved pages documents a national farmer registry for Egypt. The only page carrying registration scale figures for Egypt's 'Farmer Card' (كارت الفلاح) agricultural-holding system is Al Mal News (almalnews.com), a T5 news outlet, which this prerequisite row explicitly bars as a source of statistics. The T1 FAO/CAPMAS pages describe decennial agricultural censuses and an agricultural property (zemam) survey, which are statistical enumerations, not an operating administrative registry of farmers; the T1 FAO regional article on farmer registries covers Morocco, Jordan and Lebanon and does not report on Egypt. The T3 ministry pages (moa.gov.eg, agri.gov.eg) contain only a passing, machine-translated news headline referencing 'farmer cards' with no description of a registry, its legal basis, coverage or operation, which is too thin to establish a rung for a gating indicator.
answer.construct_note: The indicator names a registry of FARMERS (individuals). The best available Egyptian evidence describes a registry of agricultural HOLDINGS (حيازات) embedded in the 'Farmer Card' (كارت الفلاح) input-subsidy smart-card scheme. As context only, and from a T5 outlet that cannot be recorded as a value here, Al Mal News (31 March 2021) reports the Minister of Agriculture stating 5.6 million holders (حائز) covering 7.2 million feddans enumerated and registered, 3.028 million cards printed, launch in 12 governorates covering more than 4 million holdings, and roughly 419,000 tonnes of fertiliser disbursed through the system — four non-comparable units (holders enumerated, cards printed, holdings, disbursements) in a single statement. Separately, the T1 FAO agricultural census metadata confirms the statistical unit in Egypt is 'the agricultural holding', not the individual farmer, reinforcing that Egypt's record sits on the holdings side of the open definitional question. Neither is a T1-T3 statement about a national farmer registry.
answer.rung_argument: No rung is proposed. None of the supplied admissible pages does any of these for Egypt. answer.value: Egypt operates a legally mandated national project to computerize (mechanize) the agricultural real-rights register (al-sijill al-'ayni al-zira'i), implementation of which is assigned to the Egyptian Survey Authority together with the Real Estate Publicity Department under Law No. 142 of 1964 and Minister of Justice Decree No. 825 of 1975.

answer.construct_note: The indicator name conflates three registers. The quoted evidence sits on the agricultural/real-rights side: the Egyptian Survey Authority's national project to mechanize the sijill 'ayni (real-rights register) for agricultural land, i.e. plot-level registration digitisation. Two adjacent bodies of evidence sit on the OTHER side of the open question and were deliberately not used as the value: (a) the World Bank's Modernization of Egyptian Property Registration Project (P177720, US$230m, Ministry of Justice), whose objective is 'to establish the foundations of a modern and efficient land administration and management system at national level and scale up property registration in selected new urban communities' — the scale-up component is explicitly urban (new urban communities), not agricultural; and (b) Law No. 88 of 2025 creating a Unified National Real Estate ID Database, which is economy-wide (land, buildings, facilities) and covers urban property, and for which the only supplied source is a T5 law-firm/news page usable for existence only. Neither of those is an agricultural plot-registration figure.
answer.rung_argument: Absent (1) is ruled out: a named national digitisation programme for the plot-level real-rights register exists on the mandated agency's own site. Announced (2) is exceeded: this is not a press announcement but a statutory arrangement — Law No. 142 of 1964 established the sijill 'ayni system, Minister of Justice Decree No. 825 of 1975 issued its executive regulations, and the quoted sentence records that implementation of the national mechanization project was formally entrusted ('وأنيط') to the Egyptian Survey Authority and the Real Estate Publicity Department. That is an adopted instrument with a named implementing authority and legal basis = Adopted, level 3. No addition for quality_evidence or scale_evidence, both left empty.
answer.negative_finding: Operating was not recorded, and in any case would not raise the level above 3: none of the supplied pages report the digital agricultural register actually processing transactions or holding registered plots — no parcels digitised, no governorate coverage, no transaction volumes. The countervailing signal is the World Bank's 2021 concept note, which states the objective is still 'to establish the foundations of a modern and efficient land administration and management system at national level', implying the modern digital foundation was not yet in place. Level 4 was not proposed because there is no independent or official evaluation, audit or performance report on how well digital land registration works in Egypt — the Land Governance Assessment PDF supplied contains only front matter (acronyms, acknowledgements) with no assessable findings text. Level 5 was not proposed because no reach figures for digital land/plot registration are published in the supplied pages. answer.source_title: FAO, Land Resources Information Systems in the Near East (Regional Workshop, Cairo, 2001) — Country report: Land and water resources information system in Egypt
answer.quote: A Geographic Information System (GIS) has been in use at EALIP since 1997, and a GIS-based soil database was used for production of maps and other related materials on soil salinity, sodicity and water table level, and on gypsum and subsoiling requirements.
answer.data_quality_flag: Primary evidence is a 2001 FAO workshop country report; no source in the retrieved set documents the current operating status, maintenance or accessibility of the database. FAO's current National Soil Information Systems inventory does not list Egypt.
answer.construct_note: The indicator's unratified question is whether a digitised legacy paper map suffices or whether an operating digital soil information service is required. The Egyptian evidence sits on BOTH sides but weakly on each. (a) Legacy side: FAO's Soil Legacy Maps page lists Egypt among countries for which archived paper maps have been scanned, but these are explicitly 'in JPF format, and are not geo-referenced' — a digital image archive, not a database. (b) Service side: FAO's inventory of National Soil Information Systems lists no Egyptian SIS (NENA region shows only Iran and Lebanon), i.e. no FAO-recognised operating national soil information service. (c) The quoted EALIP GIS-based soil database is a genuine national soil database, but it is thematically restricted to soil-degradation attributes (salinity, sodicity, water-table depth, gypsum and subsoiling requirements) rather than a full national soil classification/property map, and the evidence dates from 2001. The related NARSS work quoted in the same volume produced 'digital soil and terrain data of Egypt in cooperation with the FAO and the European Soil Bureau', again undated as to current status.

Adopted (3) is supported: an institutionally owned national soil database exists within a mandated government body (EALIP, Ministry of Agriculture and Land Reclamation), with country-wide map products described in the FAO country report. answer.construct_note: The figure is Egypt's ITU Global Cybersecurity Index (GCI) 2024 overall score, which is the construct the indicator names. Two caveats bear on the unratified definition: (a) GCI 2024 is scored out of 100 (five pillars of 20 points each), while this register's cut points (0.2/0.4/0.6/0.8) are written on a 0-1 basis — the two are commensurable only after dividing by 100 (Egypt = 1.00), and the register's Nigeria entry of 0.824 appears to be on the 0-1 scale while Egypt's 100 is on the 0-100 scale; (b) the ITU GCI 2024 pages retrieved here (itu.int publication landing page and the GCI programme page) do not display a per-country overall score, so the only quotable figure for Egypt in the supplied material is the Egyptian regulator's statement of 100 points and Tier 1 ("role modelling") classification. Separately, GCI measures national cybersecurity commitment generally, not agriculture-sector cybersecurity.
answer.quality_evidence: The value is an ITU GCI score attributed by Egypt's telecom regulator (NTRA/EG-CERT), the national GCI focal point. It is corroborated in substance by the ITU GCI programme page describing the five-pillar aggregate score methodology, and by a T5 news account (Egyptian Gazette) stating Egypt was "among the top 12 countries on the Global Cybersecurity Index (GCI) in 2023 and 2024 Egypt scoring 100 points". answer.scale_evidence: GCI is a national-level (whole-of-country) measure covering legal, technical, organizational, capacity development and cooperation pillars; Egypt is placed in Tier 1 of 5, one of 46-47 countries at that tier out of 193 ITU member states.
answer.rung_argument: Route taken: a single published figure exists for the named construct. Value: 100 points on the GCI 2024 (equivalently 1.00 on a 0-1 basis). Construct: the source names the ITU Global Cybersecurity Index explicitly, for Egypt, for the 2023-2024 edition, and the score is the aggregate across the five GCI pillars — this is the indicator's named construct, not a proxy. Applying the cut points arithmetically: 1.00 clears 0.2 (level 2), 0.4 (level 3), 0.6 (level 4) and 0.8 (level 5). Institutional corroboration that the score is not hollow: a National Cybersecurity Strategy 2023-2027 published by MCIT, an operating national CERT (EG-CERT) under NTRA, and ITU's own historical page recording Egypt's long-standing GCI participation.
answer.negative_finding: Level 5 is the top rung, so no higher level was withheld. The residual doubt that would matter to an auditor is directional rather than level-changing: the maximum score is quoted from the assessed government's own regulator, not from the ITU GCI 2024 report itself, which was not retrievable in the supplied pages; and the score measures cybersecurity commitment instruments (laws, strategies, CERT, cooperation), not measured cyber-resilience outcomes or any agriculture-sector-specific cybersecurity provision.

The value itself is well evidenced: a T3 government source states the exact number for the named index, the named edition, and this country, and it is corroborated by two independent secondary reports of the same edition.

answer.abstain_reason: The only figures in the supplied pages for Egypt measure TOTAL tertiary gross enrolment across all fields of study (World Bank WDI SE.TER.ENRR, sourced from UNESCO UIS), not the STEM subset named by this indicator. The two UNdata series that do concern science programmes (share of tertiary graduates from science programmes, and count of tertiary graduates from science programmes) list Egypt in their reference-area filter menus but the retrieved page text contains no Egypt observation rows — only rows for Afghanistan through Angola/Anguilla — so no STEM figure for Egypt can be quote-verified from the supplied evidence. Recording the total tertiary GER against thresholds calibrated for a STEM share would convert a data gap into a confident high score.
answer.construct_note: Context only, not recorded as the cell value: World Bank WDI 'School enrollment, tertiary (% gross)' (SE.TER.ENRR, https://data.worldbank.org/indicator/SE.TER.ENRR?locations=EG) lists Egypt, Arab Rep. at a most-recent value of 38 for 2025; the female series on the Gender Data Portal gives 38.6% for 2025; IndexMundi (T5 mirror) gives 38.90 for 2018. All of these are the gross enrolment ratio for ALL tertiary education regardless of field — the WDI long definition is 'the ratio of total enrollment, regardless of age, to the population of the age group that officially corresponds to the level of education shown' — with no restriction to science, technology, engineering or mathematics. The indicator name as written asserts the STEM subset; the available evidence sits on the wrong side of that open definitional question. A STEM-specific measure would additionally be a share-of-enrolment or share-of-graduates figure (UIS series such as FOSGP_56_F400), which is a different denominator from a gross enrolment ratio and would not be comparable against the 10/20/30/40 cut points in the same way.
answer.quality_evidence: The total-tertiary figures come from T1 publishers (World Bank WDI drawing on UNESCO Institute for Statistics via the UIS API, date published 2026-02) and are methodologically well documented, but they are documented as covering tertiary education as a whole. The UNdata science-programme series are also T1 (UIS Data Centre) but the supplied extracts contain no Egypt rows and the series were last updated in UNdata in 2016.
answer.scale_evidence: No STEM enrolment or STEM graduate magnitude for Egypt appears anywhere in the supplied pages — neither a percentage nor a headcount.
answer.rung_argument: No level is proposed. A threshold score here would have to rest on the 38 (2025) total tertiary GER, which passes the 30 cut and would mechanically yield level 4. That arithmetic is sound only if the value measures the construct named in the row, and it does not: it is enrolment across all fields, not the STEM subset. Egypt's STEM share of tertiary enrolment is certainly a fraction of the total, so the total-based score would be an upper bound of unknown tightness, not a measurement. Level withheld pending either ratification of the row's definition as total tertiary GER (in which case the WDI 38 for 2025 is directly usable) or retrieval of a UIS STEM-share figure for Egypt.

answer.data_quality_flag: Launch announcement by implementing agency; no independent verification of subsequent deployment status
answer.construct_note: The FAO/MoALR initiative is explicitly a digital model of agricultural extension delivered through a mobile application to MoALR extension personnel and farmers, which is the named construct. answer.rung_argument: Absent is ruled out: two FAO T1 pages document Egyptian digital agricultural advisory/awareness tools (the MoALR-FAO digital extension model, 2019; the AMAN poultry app and web platform, 2017). answer.negative_finding: Operating was not proposed because none of the supplied pages shows the digital extension model actually delivering advisory services after launch: the FAO release describes content conversion, training of trainers and farmer awareness sessions in the future tense ('will work closely... to convert the technical content into digital content', 'will be delivered to MoALR extension personnel'), and no later page reports the application in live use by extension agents or farmers. quality_evidence was left empty because the only assessment text available (FAO policy brief on rural advisory services in Egypt) evaluates the extension system's general coverage — noting 'the weakened coverage of extension and rural advisory services' — and contains no evaluation, audit or performance report of a digital extension service. scale_evidence was left empty because no user, subscriber, governorate-coverage or beneficiary figures for any Egyptian digital extension service appear in the pages; the '2.5 million small poultry farms' figure in the AMAN page is a national farm-population denominator, not AMAN registrations.

5.4.name: Digital literacy among farmers (%)

answer.abstain_reason: No supplied source publishes a digital-literacy rate among farmers for Egypt. The only quantified evidence (IFPRI/CGIAR Discussion Paper 02359 and its 2024 policy note) is a baseline self-reported barrier ranking from a randomized trial covering ~4,000 GIZ-supported smallholders in two governorates (Minya and Beni Suef), and its headline digital-capability figure is the share citing digital ILliteracy as a key obstacle — the inverse of the indicator's direction, from a purposive, non-representative, sub-national sample. Recording it as a national digital-literacy percentage would convert a data gap into a confident score.
answer.construct_note: Indicator names a national percentage of farmers who are digitally literate (higher is better). Closest evidence: IFPRI Policy Note (Sept 2024) / IFPRI Discussion Paper 02359 (Sept 2025) on a randomized digital-literacy intervention in Minya and Beni Suef. Its baseline survey of roughly 4,000 GIZ Agricultural Innovation Project farmers reports that 52 percent named general digital literacy as a key challenge to using mobile applications, 54 percent named unawareness of existing applications, 49 percent lack of smartphone access, and about 65 percent proposed digital literacy training as the remedy. The note also states 2,400 of the 4,000 farmers own smartphones and that non-smartphone owners were excluded from the trial. These are (a) self-reported obstacle rankings, not a tested or assessed literacy rate; (b) framed as illiteracy/barrier prevalence, the inverse of the indicator's H direction; (c) drawn from two Upper Egypt governorates and from members of donor-supported farmer organizations, so not a national farmer population estimate. Contextual only — not recorded as the cell value.
answer.quality_evidence: The IFPRI/CGIAR papers are T2 (international-organisation analytical research, RCT registered as AEARCTR-0012723) and are methodologically credible for their own purpose, but their purpose is impact evaluation of a training intervention, not measurement of a population digital-literacy rate. The discussion paper is explicitly labelled preliminary and not externally peer-reviewed via IFPRI's Publications Review Committee. No T1 Egyptian source (CAPMAS, MCIT, MALR) in the retrieved set publishes farmer digital literacy; the ITU WSIS+10 Egypt country report covers national ICT capacity-building programmes without any farmer-level literacy statistic. The Mansour (2023, Library Hi Tech) study of 131 farmers in Qena is qualitative on ICT use and cites illiteracy as an influencing factor, with no digital-literacy percentage in the retrieved abstract.
answer.scale_evidence: Geographic scope of the best evidence is two governorates (Minya, Beni Suef) and a sampling frame of about 4,000 farmers in roughly 30 donor-supported farmer organizations; national coverage is absent. Egypt has millions of agricultural holders, so this frame is a small, purposively selected fraction and cannot be scaled to a national rate.
answer.rung_argument: No level is proposed. Level assignment on this threshold scale requires a percentage of farmers who ARE digitally literate. The available number (52 percent citing digital illiteracy as a barrier) cannot be inverted into 48 percent literate: it is a multiple-response obstacle ranking, not a complement of a literacy measure, and it comes from a two-governorate donor-project sample. Assigning any level from it — level 3 by naive inversion, or level 4 from the 2,400/4,000 smartphone-ownership share — would attribute to the row a national statistic that no publisher has produced.
answer.negative_finding: Not applicable in the usual sense because no level is proposed; the specific gap is that no source in the retrieved set states, for Egypt, a percentage of farmers assessed or reporting as digitally literate at national scope, in the positive direction the indicator names. Even the lowest rung (below 10 percent) cannot be evidenced, since the sub-national data suggest capability well above that but do not measure it.
answer.search_trail: 1) FAO e-Agriculture Egypt digital extension news (T1) — describes FAO/MoALR digital extension model and farmer awareness sessions; no literacy statistic. 2) FAO geodata farmers' toolkit Egypt page — 404, no content. 3) FAO family farming item — Cloudflare bot-check page, no content. 4) FAO DVI Readiness Assessment — defines a 'digital literacy' criterion for rural communities but is a generic Europe/Central Asia tool with no Egypt value. 5) ITU WSIS+10 Egypt country reporting (T1) — ICT capacity-building narrative across action lines; no farmer digital literacy figure in the retrieved text. 6+7) IFPRI Discussion Paper 02359 full text (CGSpace, T2) — abstract and introduction give intervention effect sizes (uptake +20pp, utilization +26pp, trust +8-13pp), not a literacy stock. 8) IFPRI Policy Note, Sept 2024 (CGSpace, T2) — the only quantified baseline: 52 percent of sampled farmers report general digital literacy as a key challenge; two governorates, ~4,000 GIZ-project farmers; inverse construct, sub-national. 9) OUCI record for Mansour (2023), ICT use among farmers in Qena — 131 farmers, qualitative findings, illiteracy cited as an influence; no percentage. 10) IFPRI Egypt SSP blog (T5) — restates the RCT abstract, effect sizes only. Dead ends: no CAPMAS/MCIT household or agricultural-census digital-skills breakdown for the farming population, and no ITU/Findex rural digital-skills series disaggregated to farmers appeared in the supplied pages. Conclusion: nothing in the retrieved set measures the named construct for Egypt; hold for ratification.

### What is the best available evidence, and what does it say?

The construct you describe matches closely the CGIAR/GIZ study **“Digital literacy training to promote diffusion of digital agricultural tools to smallholder farmers: Evidence from a randomized intervention in Egypt”** and its associated technical materials.[1][2][3][5][6]

- The study is a **randomized controlled trial (RCT)** evaluating *digital literacy training* and promotion strategies to increase the diffusion of digital agricultural technologies among **smallholder farmers in Egypt**.[1][3][5]  
- The **target population** is smallholder farmers in **two governorates of Upper Egypt: Minya and Beni Suef**.[1][3]  
- A **baseline phone survey** was conducted **between July and September 2023**

answer.value: WIPO's Global Innovation Index 2025 places Egypt 86th of 139 economies (input sub-index rank 94, output sub-index rank 81), with published GII pillar scores on the 0-100 scale of 39.1 Institutions, 21.1 Human capital and research, 35.3 Infrastructure, 32.2 Market sophistication, 25.3 Business sophistication, 16.9 Knowledge and technology outputs and 20.7 Creative outputs; the headline composite GII score itself is not printed on any of the retrieved WIPO pages.
answer.unit: GII rank (of 139) and GII pillar scores, 0-100
answer.source_title: WIPO, Egypt Ranking in the Global Innovation Index 2025 (GII economy page and economy profile)
answer.quote: Egypt ranks 86th among the 139 economies featured in the GII 2025.
answer.data_quality_flag: Headline GII composite score for Egypt is not printed in the retrieved pages; only the rank and the seven pillar scores are published there. The implied composite sits within roughly one point of the level-1/level-2 cut point, so the level is boundary-sensitive.
answer.construct_note: The source is the named construct (WIPO Global Innovation Index, Egypt), but it publishes Egypt's RANK (86th of 139) and its seven PILLAR scores rather than the single overall GII score in points that this threshold indicator's cut points (25/35/45/55) are written against. No overall score figure appears verbatim in any supplied page, so none is recorded as a number.
answer.quality_evidence: WIPO is the publisher of the GII; the economy page and economy profile are the official GII 2025 outputs for Egypt, with a stated confidence interval for the rank (ranks 81-88) and a full indicator-level table. The same rank (86th) is corroborated across the 2025 PDF brief, the interactive economy page and the 2024 brief, and independently repeated in a T5 secondary write-up.
answer.scale_evidence: Egypt is covered in full: all seven pillars and nearly all ~80 indicators carry scores and ranks in the GII 2025 economy profile, with only two indicators marked n/a (PISA scales; cultural and creative services exports). Coverage extends back through 2020 in the published ranking series (96th, 94th, 89th, 86th, 86th, 86th).
answer.rung_argument: Level 1 (below 25 points): the only scores WIPO publishes for Egypt on the retrieved pages are the seven pillar scores. Five of the seven sit at or below 35.3 and the two output pillars are 16.9 and 20.7; the highest single pillar is Institutions at 39.1. On the GII's own construction the composite is the mean of the input sub-index (mean of the five input pillars) and the output sub-index (mean of the two output pillars), which from the published pillar scores places Egypt's composite in the mid-20s, i.e. at or just below the first cut point of 25. Egypt's rank of 86th out of 139, 15th of 18 in Northern Africa and Western Asia, and its position 'at expectations' relative to GDP are all consistent with a composite in that band rather than higher. Because no published composite figure appears in the supplied pages, the value is recorded as a statement and the level is argued rather than computed from a quoted number.
answer.negative_finding: Level 2 would require evidence of a GII score above 25 points. The only agriculture-side training in the supplied pages (FAO/MALR Training of Trainers and a digital skills course for extension agents) is basic digital literacy and app usage, not data science, and carries no cohort or pipeline figures. Because the indicator name joins 'agtech' and 'data-science' with an unratified slash, and the best evidence sits entirely on the data-science side with the agriculture bridge explicitly absent, the cell is held pending definition ratification rather than scored off a generic ICT programme.

answer.data_quality_flag: Ministry self-reported programme figures in a press release; no independent evaluation in the supplied pages
answer.construct_note: The named construct is an agtech/data-science training pipeline. What is published for Egypt in these pages is (a) a generic national data/ICT talent pipeline with no agricultural component and (b) agricultural digital-literacy training with no data-science component. For context only, and quoted exactly from the MCIT pages: 'Furthermore, 13,800 out of 25,000 individuals were trained within the Digital Egypt Pioneers Initiative (DEPI). It aims to enhance the digital skills of university students and graduates across different specializations by delivering specialized educational tracks in Artificial Intelligence (AI), data analysis, cybersecurity, and programming.' and 'Around 500,000 trainees received digital capacity-building training during FY 2024-25, with a target of reaching 800,000 trainees in the current fiscal year.' Neither statement mentions agriculture, agrifood, agronomy or an agtech track. On the other side of the slash, FAO Egypt reports 'Training of Trainers (ToT) programs on the thematic areas and use of the mobile application will be delivered to MoALR extension personnel' and a five-day digital skills course for extension agents covering 'Word, YouTube, e-mail, Facebook, WhatsApp, Zoom and the FAO app El Mufeed' — agriculture-situated, but digital literacy rather than data science, and with no enrolment, graduate or pipeline figures. If the slash is later ratified as disjunctive (either half suffices), the MCIT DEPI evidence would support an Operating rung with scale; if conjunctive (an agtech-specific data-science pipeline), the supplied evidence supports Absent-to-Announced. That fork is exactly the unresolved question flagged in the indicator census, so no level is proposed.
answer.rung_argument: No rung is asserted because the rung would be determined by the unratified reading of the indicator name. Under a conjunctive reading (agtech-specific data-science training), nothing in the supplied pages evidences a named, funded or enrolled programme, so the rung would be Absent (1). Under a disjunctive reading, MCIT's DEPI is demonstrably Operating with published cohort numbers, which with scale_evidence filled would reach 4. Recording either as if settled would either understate or inflate the row; the honest record is a hold at 0.
answer.negative_finding: No level was proposed at all. Specifically, level 3+ was not proposed because no supplied page shows an adopted or operating training programme that names agriculture, agrifood or agtech as a track, specialisation, cohort or partner; and quality_evidence was withheld because the only performance language available is the Ministry's own statement that 'standards and criteria are being developed to ensure training quality' — a statement of intent about design, not an evaluation or audit result. answer.abstain_reason: None of the retrieved pages publishes any figure for the share of women (or gender composition) in Egypt's digital-agriculture workforce — whether defined as extension staff, agtech-company employees, or ICT-in-agriculture roles. The available Egyptian figures measure adjacent but different constructs (female labour force participation overall, women's share of agricultural employment, gender gap in internet use), so recording any of them here would substitute a different construct for the named one.
answer.construct_note: The closest Egyptian evidence retrieved sits on the wrong side of the census question. Egypt's Ministry of Planning and Economic Development (T3) reports that 'The agricultural sector employs 45% of women in the labor force (while only 24% for men)' — that is the share of employed women who work in agriculture, not women's share of any digital-agriculture occupation, and it coincidentally sits on a threshold cut point, which makes mis-recording it especially dangerous. The same page reports a gender gap in internet use (women 47%, men 69%) — a general connectivity statistic, not a workforce composition. The World Bank feature (T1) gives female labour force participation of 'around 18%' economy-wide. The FAO story (T1) documents a MALR/FAO digital-skills course for extension agents with named women trainers and trainees but gives no sex-disaggregated count or percentage of extension staff. The GIZ Gender Value Chain Assessment PDFs returned only tables of contents, with a section titled 'Access to information technology and mobile usage' but no extracted figures; the CGIAR GENDER paper on social equity in Egypt's digital agriculture transformation returned an access-denied page and could not be quote-verified. No admissible source in the retrieved set defines or measures a 'digital-ag workforce' for Egypt at all.
answer.quality_evidence: Two T1 pages (World Bank feature, FAO story), one T3 page (Egyptian Ministry of Planning and Economic Development news item), two T4 GIZ PDFs available only as front matter, one T2 CGIAR page that returned an administrative block, and one ILO catalogue page that returned HTTP 410. Only the T3 ministry page carries any agriculture-plus-gender-plus-digital statistics, and those are economy-wide or sector-wide, not workforce-composition figures for digital agriculture.
answer.scale_evidence: No denominator for a 'digital-ag workforce' exists in any retrieved source — no count of extension officers by sex, no agtech employer survey, no ICT-in-agriculture occupational breakdown from CAPMAS or ILOSTAT. Without a defined population, no share can be computed or verified.
answer.rung_argument: No level is proposed. The threshold ladder (20/35/45/50) presupposes a published percentage for women's share of the digital-agriculture workforce. The retrieved evidence contains no such percentage, so there is no value to test against the first cut of 20. Assigning even level 1 would imply an evidenced finding that the share is below 20%, which the sources do not establish; assigning level 3 on the basis of the 45% agricultural-employment figure would import a different construct across the definitional boundary the indicator census itself flags as unresolved. The level is therefore withheld pending ratification of the construct definition and identification of a source that measures it.
answer.negative_finding: Level 1 was not proposed because that would assert an evidenced share below 20%; nothing in the retrieved pages establishes any share, high or low, for women in Egypt's digital-agriculture workforce. What any level would require — a sex-disaggregated headcount or percentage for a defined digital-ag population (MALR extension cadre, agtech firm employment, or ICT-in-agriculture occupational codes) — is absent from every source retrieved.

6.13.name: SME/agribusiness adoption of digital tools (%)

answer.abstain_reason: No admissible source in the retrieved pages publishes a percentage for adoption of digital tools by Egyptian SMEs/agribusinesses as named. The only percentage on point (53% of SMEs having adopted digital payments, from a Visa/MSMEDA study) appears solely in an Ahram Online news article (T5), and T5 material may carry existence facts only, never a statistic; it also measures a narrower tool class (payments) for economy-wide SMEs rather than agribusiness firms. The one T2 source that does sit on the agribusiness side (ICARDA, 'Current Situation of Digital Agriculture in Egypt') is qualitative only — it names which tool categories are 'fairly widely used' and what constrains SME adoption, but publishes no adoption rate, and the full report is Limited Access so the finding cannot be quote-verified beyond the abstract. The indicator's own definition is unratified on both the population (SMEs vs agribusiness) and on what counts as a 'digital tool', so the available evidence cannot be mapped onto it without inventing a figure.
answer.construct_note: Best available quantified evidence: Ahram Online (T5, 16 Sep 2025) reports a Visa/MSMEDA study finding 'Around 53 percent of SMEs have integrated digital payments' in Egypt, with 77% of SME owners expecting electronic transactions to be central to growth. That figure (a) is economy-wide SMEs, not agribusiness firms, (b) covers digital payments only, not the broader 'digital tools' the indicator names, and (c) reaches us only through a news outlet, i.e. an inadmissible tier for a statistic. A second partial measure, World Bank Enterprise Survey 2008 for Egypt (T1), shows 421 of 1,156 firms (36.4%) regularly using a website in interactions with clients, but the ES universe explicitly excludes agriculture ('non-agricultural formal private economy', and the 2025 round covers ISIC Rev.4 10-33 manufacturing plus listed services), the page itself warns the counts 'cannot be interpreted as summary statistics of the population of interest', and the figure is 17 years old. Neither sits on the agribusiness side of the undefined slash.
answer.quality_evidence: ICARDA (T2, 2023, CGSpace) 'Current Situation of Digital Agriculture in Egypt' is the only retrieved source addressing the named construct on the agribusiness side: its abstract states that of 8 categories of digital agriculture tools, only sensors and mobile apps are fairly widely used in Egypt, and that mobile connectivity, data security concerns, farmer knowledge levels and inflation constrain further adoption of DA tools by SMEs. This is a directional, qualitative finding with no rate attached; the item is marked 'Limited Access', so nothing beyond the abstract can be verified. IFPRI MENA Working Paper 43 (Abdelaziz & Tarek 2024, indexed on FAO AGRIS) likewise characterises adoption of digital agricultural tools as low and uneven and studies constraints among Egyptian smallholder farmers — farmers, not agribusiness SMEs — and the retrieved record carries only the abstract, no adoption percentage.
answer.scale_evidence: No population-scaled adoption estimate for Egyptian agribusiness firms was found. The Visa/MSMEDA 53% figure, if it were admissible, would apply to SMEs across all sectors (SMEs are stated to make up 98% of Egypt's private sector); no sectoral breakdown for agriculture/agribusiness was published in the retrieved page.
answer.rung_argument: Level withheld. A threshold score here would require a published adoption rate for the named population (SMEs and/or agribusiness firms) and the named tool class (digital tools). The retrieved evidence offers three non-substitutable fragments: a T5-only 53% for digital payments among all-sector SMEs; a T1 microdata frequency (36.4% website use, 2008) drawn from a non-agricultural universe and expressly disclaimed as not a population statistic; and a T2 qualitative characterisation of digital-agriculture tool use among Egyptian SMEs with no number. Choosing any of these as the cell value would either cross the construct boundary the indicator names or manufacture a precision the sources do not have, so no rung — including rung 1 — is asserted.
answer.negative_finding: Level 1 was not proposed either, because proposing it would assert that agribusiness/SME digital tool adoption in Egypt is below 10%, and nothing in the retrieved evidence establishes that: ICARDA reports that two of eight digital-agriculture tool categories (sensors and mobile apps) are already 'fairly widely used', and the (inadmissible) SME payments figure is 53%. The specific missing item that any level would require is a published, tier-admissible adoption rate whose denominator is Egyptian SMEs or agribusiness firms and whose numerator is use of digital tools.

3.10.name: Agricultural e-commerce platforms

answer.value: Farmer-facing agricultural e-commerce platforms are operating in Egypt, including Nile, a B2B online marketplace that connects fresh produce growers directly with commercial buyers, and Bashaier, a mobile marketplace linking small-scale farmers to buyers.
answer.source_title: FAO Science, Technology and Innovation (STI) Portal / ATIO Knowledge Base — "Nile online marketplace" innovation record
answer.quote: Nile online marketplace is a B2B platform designed to connect fresh produce growers directly with commercial buyers. It streamlines the wholesale process by offering a digital space where producers can list their products and buyers can browse, order, and manage purchases efficiently.
answer.data_quality_flag: FAO STI Portal record is a federated entry harvested from Digital Agri Hub and enriched by automated AI extraction; the page itself states "Newly extracted from original record - Not checked, not enriched", so the platform description is not independently verified by FAO staff.
answer.construct_note: The indicator census asks whether the row counts only farmer-facing platforms or any agri-food value-chain commerce platform. The evidence quoted (Nile) sits on the farmer-facing side: growers list produce and sell directly to commercial buyers. The second FAO record (Bashaier, https://sti-portal.fao.org/innovations/kef-bashaier-egypt) is likewise farmer-facing. The only Egyptian platform in the retrieved pages with published reach figures is Cartona (cartona.com, T5 vendor page: "150,000+ RETAIL USERS", "4,500+ SUPPLIERS", "18 CITIES"), but Cartona is an FMCG retailer-to-wholesaler B2B marketplace serving mom-and-pop stores, i.e. downstream agri-food trade rather than a farmer-facing agricultural platform, and it is a vendor self-report at T5, which may carry existence facts but not statistics. No figures for Nile or Bashaier were found in the retrieved pages.
answer.rung_argument: Absent is ruled out: the FAO STI Portal carries country-tagged Egyptian records for at least two agricultural e-commerce/marketplace innovations (Nile, Bashaier). Announced is exceeded: these are not stated intentions but described as existing platforms with live URLs (nile.ag; a Google Play listing for Bashaier). Adopted is exceeded: the Nile record classifies the innovation stage as "Mature" and readiness as "9. Ready", and the Bashaier record describes an app available on the Google Play Store and "actively serving users in Egypt" — i.e. transacting in the open market rather than merely procured or piloted. Hence Operating = 3. Both add-on fields are left empty, so the level stays at 3.
answer.negative_finding: Level 4 was not proposed because no independent or official evaluation, audit, service-standard report or performance assessment of any Egyptian agricultural e-commerce platform appears in the retrieved pages. The FAO STI Portal readiness/adoption narratives are AI-generated restatements of the platforms' own descriptions (the page itself flags "Harvested + Automated AI", "Not checked, not enriched"), which is design/self-description, not quality evidence. The only independent analytical text retrieved, the IFPRI/CGIAR policy note, speaks to the digital-agriculture app ecosystem as a whole rather than evaluating e-commerce platform performance, and its finding is that "many Egyptian digital tools remain pilot-stage or region-specific, with very few achieving national scale" — the opposite of a positive performance record. Level 5 was not proposed because no published reach figures (registered growers, transaction volumes, geographic coverage) exist for the farmer-facing platforms in these pages; the only reach numbers available belong to Cartona, a T5 vendor page for a retailer-facing FMCG marketplace, which is inadmissible both on tier and on construct.

Checked FAO e-Agriculture Egypt items (2019 digital extension model; 2017 AMAN poultry app) — both concern advisory/disease reporting, not e-commerce, so they were dead ends for this construct. Checked the FAO Investment Centre digital agriculture page — generic global text, no Egypt e-commerce figure. Checked the CGIAR/IFPRI policy note "Digital Agricultural Technology in Egypt: Insights from App Developers" (T2) — it discusses digital marketplaces and names Hodhod, Mahsooly and The Smart Farmer Guide, and reports that few Egyptian tools reach national scale, but gives no platform count or reach statistic for e-commerce specifically. Checked the GSMA 2019 agri e-commerce report (T4) — the retrieved text covers Sub-Saharan Africa, Asia and Latin America and contains no Egypt figure. Checked cartona.com (T5) — carries reach numbers but is a vendor page and a retailer-facing FMCG marketplace, so recorded only as construct context, not as the value or as scale evidence. No published count of Egyptian agricultural e-commerce platforms, and no reach or evaluation data for farmer-facing platforms, was found in the supplied pages.

answer.data_quality_flag: Qualitative, interview-based policy note; contains no user counts, registration figures or coverage statistics for any named Egyptian advisory platform
answer.construct_note: The indicator names 'digital advisory platforms AT SCALE'. No source in this set publishes a registered-user, active-user or farmers-reached figure for any Egyptian advisory platform, so the unratified '>10k user' bar cannot be tested either way. The one large number in the retrieved pages — '2 million cards were distributed to farmers' for the smart farmer card (Daily News Egypt, T5) — is a subsidy/identity card, not an advisory platform, and is a news source and therefore inadmissible for a statistic.

Ready'; Daily News Egypt records the pilot launch of Hudhud by two ministries. Adopted/Operating (3): services are live and delivering content to farmers, and GeoAgro-Misr is described as transitioning to government ownership within national extension structures, so the rung is Operating. The rung yields base level 3; neither adder is claimed, so the level stands at 3.
answer.negative_finding: Level 4 was not proposed because no independent or official evaluation, audit or performance report on how well any Egyptian advisory platform works appears in the retrieved evidence — the FAO Country Cases and STI Portal entries are implementer/self-reported descriptions (the STI Portal adoption narratives are explicitly AI-generated and in one case state that the underlying description is empty), and the only independent assessment (IFPRI) is negative about scaling, not a positive performance finding. Level 5 was not proposed because no reach figures at all are published for Egypt in these sources: no user counts, no farmer numbers, no governorate coverage. 7.12.name: Responsible-AI safeguards (consent, rights)

answer.value: Egypt has adopted a cross-sector responsible-AI safeguards regime — the Egyptian Charter for Responsible AI (2023, National Council for AI) and the National AI Governance Framework (ECRAI/NCAI, March 2026) — which asserts individual rights such as the right to know one is interacting with an AI system and to challenge adverse AI outcomes, but contains no agriculture- or farmer-specific consent or rights provisions.
answer.source_title: National Council for Artificial Intelligence (Egypt), Egyptian Charter for Responsible AI, 2023 v1.0 (ai.gov.eg)
answer.quote: Any end-user using an AI system has the fundamental right to know when he or she is interacting with an AI system and not a human being, for example in the case of automated call centers. [Transparency and Explainability]
answer.data_quality_flag: Non-binding charter; the Charter itself states most such international guidelines are non-binding and that it is a "soft launch"
answer.construct_note: The evidence sits on the cross-sector side of the unresolved definitional question. The Charter and the 2026 National AI Governance Framework are economy-wide instruments issued by the National Council for AI / ECRAI; nothing in the retrieved pages establishes agriculture- or farmer-specific consent or data-rights safeguards (e.g. consent for farm data collection, farmer data ownership). The Charter's rights language covers end-users of AI systems generally; 'consent' as such is not articulated in the quoted Charter text and is carried instead by the Personal Data Protection Law, which the Framework lists as a foundation but which was not retrieved here. If the indicator is later ratified as requiring agriculture-specific safeguards, this row should fall to Absent.
answer.rung_argument: Absent is excluded: a named, published national instrument on responsible AI exists (Egyptian Charter for Responsible AI, ai.gov.eg, 2023). Announced is exceeded: the Charter is not a plan but an issued document, launched by the National Council for AI at its seventh meeting under the ICT Minister (MCIT press release, 20 April 2023), and it has since been superseded/extended by the Guide to Egypt's National AI Governance Framework, Edition 2.0, marked 'Status: Approved for Publication' and 'NCAI Final Release', authorized by the Minister of Communications and Information Technology. Adopted is therefore established: formal, authorized, published instruments containing rights-bearing safeguards (right to know one is interacting with an AI system; mechanisms to challenge adverse AI outcomes; protection of vulnerable groups). Level for Adopted = 3, with no additive fields filled.
answer.negative_finding: Operating was not proposed: the retrieved pages contain only statements of what the instruments require (e.g. that government AI projects 'should be supervised by' MCIT and that MCIT 'presents periodically a report'), which is design language in a non-binding charter, with no retrieved record of a completed impact assessment, an enforcement action, a redress case, or a compliance report actually produced. Even if Operating were granted, the mechanical level would remain 3.
